children.text: For most Florida backyards, aluminum. Not because wood is a poor material, but because the two fail in different places, and Florida is unusually hard on the places where wood fails: humidity that never fully dries out, an insect population that eats cellulose year round, and sun that works on a finish every day of the year. A wood pergola here is a structure you maintain on a schedule. An aluminum one is a structure you inspect.

The exception is real, and it is worth naming in the first paragraph rather than burying it: if what you want is the mass and grain of heavy timber — deep beams, visible joinery, a pavilion rather than a frame — aluminum does not give you that. Choosing aluminum to get a timber look is how people end up disappointed by a perfectly sound structure.
What actually ages a pergola here
None of the three loads that matter is weight.
Water that does not leave.
Afternoon storms, overnight humidity, and irrigation overspray hitting the base of a post every morning. It is the sustained wetting, not the rain itself, that does the work.
Ultraviolet light.
It degrades the finish, not the structure — but on a roofless frame the finish is the whole game, because there is nothing above it casting shade on itself.
Uplift.
A pergola carries almost no gravity load. What it has to resist is wind trying to lift it off its footings, which is a completely different problem from holding something up.
Those three set the comparison. Everything below is a consequence of them.
The material changes the layout, not just the finish
This is the part most comparisons skip, and it is the one that changes what your yard looks like.

Aluminum is far stiffer and stronger per square inch than construction softwood, so the beam that does a given job is slimmer to begin with. It is also an extrusion, which means wall thickness is a variable an engineer can set: the same outside dimension can be specified to carry a longer clear opening by putting more metal into the section. Timber has neither lever. A solid beam that has to span further has to get deeper, or a post has to appear.

The practical version: for the same clear opening over a dining table, wood tends to want either a visibly deeper beam or an extra post somewhere you did not plan for. That post is not a detail. It lands in the middle of a seating area, or in front of the view, or exactly where the grill was going.
So the material choice happens before the layout is fixed, not after.
Seven pergola design decisions to make before construction starts
covers the rest of that sequence.
Maintenance is an overhead job, and that is the whole point
A wood pergola has to be cleaned and refinished on a repeating schedule. That sounds manageable, because most people picture refinishing a deck.
It is not a deck. It is a ceiling.
The face that shows wear first and looks worst when it goes is the
underside

of the beams and slats — the one you look at from the chairs, the one you cannot reach without a ladder, and the one where finish has to be applied upward against gravity. It is also the face that dries slowest, because it never sees direct sun.

That asymmetry is the honest version of the maintenance argument. The question is not whether you are willing to maintain wood. It is whether you, or someone you pay, will still be willing to do an overhead job on a ladder in year eight, when the novelty has gone and the structure looks fine from the seating area.

blog.alt: Timber pavilion with a gable roof, its exposed trusses joined by black steel plates and hung with ceiling fans, covering an outdoor kitchen with two built-in grills, four bar stools and a herringbone wood back wall.

children.text: Aluminum is not maintenance-free. It fails somewhere else.
Any page that says "zero maintenance" is selling. Factory-finished aluminum has its own failure modes, and they are worth knowing so you can inspect for the right things:
The coating, at the cut ends and the fastener penetrations.
A factory finish is applied to a whole extrusion. Everywhere the installer cut or drilled is a place where the coating meets bare metal, and those are the points to look at.
Chalking and fade under sustained UV.
Slow, gradual, and a function of the coating rather than the metal.
The hardware.

Fixings tend to need attention before the beams do, especially near salt air, where dissimilar metals in contact set up galvanic corrosion. On a waterfront lot the metallurgy of the screws is a more consequential specification than anything about the beams.

blog.alt: Dark aluminum pergola with a slatted top beside a pool on a canal-front lot, marble paving underfoot, black landscape uplights set in the rock bed to the right and palms lining the far bank.

children.text: The maintenance is real but it is rare and at eye level: rinse it, and once a year look at the fixings and the cut ends. Nothing about that requires a ladder and a brush.
Wood moves with moisture. Aluminum moves with heat.
Both materials move, which surprises people who expect metal to be static.

Wood takes on and gives up moisture continuously, and swells and shrinks as it does. Over enough cycles, fasteners work loose, joints open, and the hardware that holds the frame square starts to need attention. That is normal behavior, not a defect, and it is why bolted steel connectors and periodic re-tightening exist.

Aluminum barely cares about moisture and moves noticeably with temperature instead, along the length of a run. On a long span the connection detail has to let that happen. When it is not allowed to, the movement goes into the fasteners instead of the joint.
The point is symmetrical:
neither material is inert, and in both cases the quality of the build shows up in the connections rather than in the members.
The failure is at the footing, not at the beam
Pergola beams rarely fail. Post-to-footing connections do.

Because uplift is the governing load, what matters is what happens where the structure meets the ground or the slab: the size and depth of the footing, the anchor into it, and the bracket that ties post to anchor. This is true for both materials, and it is the line on the drawing worth asking about.
It also means one decision rewrites the whole calculation.
An open frame lets wind through. A frame with a canopy, fabric, louvers or screens on it does not.

The moment you add a surface, the pergola becomes something the wind pushes on, and the engineering behind it has to have assumed that from the start. Retrofitting a cover onto a structure designed as an open frame is the expensive version of that conversation.
If a solid, adjustable roof is closer to what you actually want, that is a different build rather than an upgrade:
pergola vs. louvered roof
is the comparison for it.
Termites, ground contact and the irrigation arc
Subterranean termites are active in Florida year round, and a wood pergola is a cellulose structure standing in their environment.
Pressure treatment resists them. Two qualifications, both of which cause real problems in real yards:
Every cut end and drilled hole exposes untreated wood
and has to be field-treated. That is a step that gets skipped when a crew is finishing on a Friday.
Copper-based treatments are corrosive to ordinary fasteners.
Wood-to-hardware compatibility is a specification, not a preference, and getting it wrong corrodes the connection from inside the timber where nobody can see it.
Then there is the detail that quietly decides the lifespan of a wood post:
where the irrigation heads spray.

A post standing in the arc of a rotor gets wet every single morning, which is a very different life from the same post standing clear of it. Walk the yard at run time before the posts are set, or move the heads.

blog.alt: Timber pavilion on a paver patio, its exposed trusses joined by black steel plates and its posts set on black metal bases, built against a white outbuilding with live oaks draped in Spanish moss behind.

celdas: Does not absorb it; the coating is what is exposed
Absorbs and releases it, and moves each time
Overspray, shade and drainage at the posts
Treatment resists; cut ends must be re-treated
Termites are active year round here
Rinse; inspect fasteners and cut ends
Clean and refinish on a schedule, overhead, underside included
Who is holding the brush in year eight
Stiffer material, and wall thickness is a variable, so fewer posts
Deeper beam or another post for the same opening
How much open floor you want underneath
The connection has to allow whichever applies
Needs attention before the beams do, especially near salt air
Must match the treatment chemistry or it corrodes unseen
Usually an engineered system with approval documentation behind it
Clean lines, slim members, even painted finish
The one row where wood wins outright

children.text: The paperwork is different, and it shows up as time
Material changes the permitting path more than it changes its difficulty.

Aluminum pergolas are commonly built from engineered systems that already carry approval documentation for their components and connections, so the submission is largely about siting the structure on your lot. A one-off timber structure is usually a set of drawings prepared and sealed for that site, which is a normal process with a normal fee — it simply takes longer to originate.
Neither is a reason to choose a material. It is a reason not to be surprised by a calendar.
Do you need a permit for a pergola in Florida
sets out how the review itself runs.
The ten-year arithmetic, honestly
Our estimator carries a single pergola line at
, shown — like every figure it produces — as a

band, and it prices the aluminum build we do. There is no wood line in that table, so there is no honest wood number to put beside it on this page. Inventing one to make the comparison look tidy would be worse than leaving the gap, because it is exactly the number a reader would take into a negotiation.
What you can compare without a second price is the shape of the spend:
Aluminum
front-loads it. The structure costs what it costs, and the obligation afterwards is inspection.
Wood
spreads it. Whatever the build comes to, it carries a recurring cost after it — materials, access equipment and labor, or your own weekends — for as long as you own the house.

Two things decide which shape suits you: how long you intend to be there, and whether the recurring work is something you will actually do or something you will pay someone else to do. If it is the latter, get a price for one round of it before you treat wood as the cheaper option, because that is the figure the comparison actually turns on and it is the one nobody asks for.
Run your own version on the
pool cost estimator
. What sits behind the base figure — span, what the posts land on, the wind load your lot carries, what runs inside the frame — is in
what changes an aluminum pergola's price
When wood is the right call
It genuinely is, in these cases:
You want heavy-timber mass.
Deep beams, exposed joinery, a pavilion that reads as architecture. Aluminum can be made to look clean and precise; it cannot be made to look heavy.
You are matching something that already exists.
A timber barn, an existing pavilion, a rural property where a slim painted frame would look out of place.
The maintenance is not a hypothetical.
Somebody in the picture already maintains wood, likes doing it, and will keep doing it.

If that is you, the conditions that make wood last here are specific and not optional: no ground contact anywhere, posts standing outside the irrigation arc, fasteners and connectors matched to the treatment chemistry, every cut end field-treated, and a refinishing schedule agreed on day one rather than discovered in year four.
How to decide in one sitting
Three questions, in this order:
Is the look you want achievable in the material, or are you choosing the material to get a look?
If it is the second, stop here — this is the only question that cannot be solved with better maintenance.
Who refinishes the underside, how often, and will they still want to in year eight?
Answer it with a name, not a shrug.
What is going under it later?
Fans, screens, heaters, a kitchen, a hanging light. Every one of those loads the structure or adds a surface for the wind, and they all belong in the engineering now rather than as a retrofit.
The broader version of that sequencing — how a pergola sits inside the rest of the yard rather than being decided on its own — is in the
outdoor living design guide for Florida homes
When you want to see how the aluminum version is built, spans and connections included, that is on the
custom aluminum pergola
page.
Finished projects
is the faster way to test the look question against something real, and a
project estimate
starts with the site visit — including where your irrigation heads are pointing.

faq.answer: The surface of a dark aluminum beam is hot to the touch in direct sun, and so is a dark-stained timber one. What you feel sitting underneath comes from how much sky the top blocks and which way the slats run, not from the material. That makes shade a design decision rather than a material decision.
faq.question: Does an aluminum pergola get hotter underneath than a wood one?

faq.answer: Either material can be engineered for the wind load a site requires, and neither survives on material alone. Uplift is carried by the connection from post to footing, which is the detail worth reading on the drawing. Adding a canopy, fabric or screens turns an open frame into a surface that catches wind, and that changes the engineering for both.
faq.question: Can a wood pergola handle Florida wind?

faq.answer: No. It is low-maintenance with a different failure mode. What ages is the coating at cut ends and fastener penetrations, and the hardware itself, rather than the structure. Near salt water the metallurgy of the fixings matters more than anything about the beams.
faq.question: Is an aluminum pergola maintenance-free?

faq.answer: It is rarely a material rule. Submissions turn on color, height, setback and what is visible from the street, so the answer is in your own documents rather than in a general preference. Our estimator carries a $1,500 line for an HOA submission, which is a reasonable sign that it is a real step and not a formality.
faq.question: Do HOAs prefer one material over the other?

children.text: The house usually decides this, not taste. Attach the pergola when the space you actually use touches the house
and

the wall behind it has something structural to bolt through. Build it freestanding when either of those is missing, or when the spot you really sit in is out in the yard. Everything else — material, roof type, finish — is a separate decision you make after this one, and material in particular is covered in
aluminum vs. wood over the long term

The reason the structural question comes first is that on something this light, the load that governs is wind trying to lift it, not weight pressing down. An attached pergola sends that uplift into the house. A freestanding one sends it into its own footings. That single difference is what turns a layout preference into an engineering constraint.

celdas: If this is true on your site
The wall has block, a tie beam or framing to bolt through, and the beam fits between the door head and the soffit
The eave is low, the wall is stucco over foam, or it is a gable end with nothing continuous at that height
Freestanding, or freestanding tucked under the eave
The place you actually sit is more than a few feet off the house
Pool plumbing, a drainfield or an easement sits where posts would land

children.text: What "attached" really means on site

A ledger, bolted through into structure: anchors into block or into the tie beam on a masonry wall, into studs or a band on a frame wall. Every one of those bolts is a hole through the weather barrier that has to be flashed and sealed so water does not end up inside the wall.
That detail is most of the job. An attached pergola is a waterproofing problem as much as a structural one, and it is where the shortcuts show up years later as a stain on the inside of the wall.

The failure we see in the field is simpler than that: a ledger lagged into fascia board, or into the foam trim under the stucco. Fascia carries a gutter. Foam trim carries nothing. Neither of them is a place to hang a structure that the wind is going to pull on.

blog.alt: Patio cover with translucent corrugated roof panels on a dark frame over a brick paver patio at the back of a tile-roofed stucco house, with french doors and two chairs underneath.

children.text: What "freestanding" really means on site

Its own footings, one under each post, sized and placed by whoever engineers the structure. The uplift goes to the ground through anchors set in that concrete. Nothing is bolted to the house, no one has to discuss what the tie-in does to a roof warranty, and the whole structure can go wherever the setbacks allow.

The price of that freedom is that you have to know what is underground. Posts landing on pool plumbing, an irrigation main, a septic drainfield or a utility easement either move the structure or stop it. That is a site walk with locates, not something you settle from a rendering.

blog.alt: Dark bronze freestanding pergola with open slats on a stone pool deck beside an infinity-edge pool, with palms around it and a canal lined with houses behind.

children.text: Five things on the house that decide it before you do
The door head

The beam of an attached pergola has to clear the top of the slider or french door it passes over, and it has to tuck under the soffit. On a single-story Florida house those two lines are often only a few inches apart. If the beam will not fit between them, attached is finished as an option — no design gets you around it.
Measure both heights before anyone draws anything. That gap is your entire attached option, expressed as a number.
What is already on the wall

Walk it and write down what is there: windows, the condenser, the electrical panel, the gas meter, the hose bib, the dryer vent. Building over a condenser means roofing over equipment that needs clearance and service access.

Building over a window means the room behind it gets permanently darker. That is the consequence homeowners discover last and regret most, and it is the reason a fair number of attached pergolas should have been set off the wall instead.
Where the roof sheds water

An attached pergola sits directly under the edge where the roof dumps. In an afternoon storm that is a sheet of water landing on the rafters and then on the deck in one line, in the same place, every time.
It is solvable with a gutter and somewhere for the water to go. It is solvable cheaply at design time and expensively afterwards, once the deck is down and the grading is set.
What is under the post locations
For a freestanding structure this is the whole feasibility study. Stake the post positions and have them located before the layout is final, not after the footings are dug.
Setbacks, lot coverage and the HOA

Both layouts are structures, and both go through permitting and inspection; what varies is where each is allowed to sit. An attached pergola usually lands inside the footprint you are already permitted to build in. A freestanding one out in the yard can walk straight into a rear or side setback.

A structure standing alone in the middle of a yard also draws more architectural comment from an HOA than one that reads as part of the house. Our estimator carries an HOA submission as a $1,500 line, which is worth knowing before it arrives as a surprise. What the review itself involves is in
do you need a permit for a pergola in Florida
The shade argument nobody makes: which way the rafters run

An open pergola only shades while the sun is high enough for the rafters to cast onto each other. In Florida that makes it a midday tool. By late afternoon the sun comes in almost sideways, under the roof entirely, and rafter direction stops mattering at all.

Attached fixes that geometry for you. The rafters span from the ledger out to the front beam, perpendicular to the wall, because that is the only way the structure works. Freestanding lets you turn the whole thing: orient the rafters against the worst sun, or set it far enough off the house that the house itself blocks the late light.

If the area you are covering faces west, understand before you commit that an open top will not solve four o'clock in either layout. That is a roof decision rather than a layout one, and it is the subject of
pergola vs. louvered roof
Height is the thing attached gives up
An attached pergola's height is dictated to you by the soffit above and the door head below. A freestanding one lets you choose it, and that choice does more work than it looks like.

Higher feels airier, moves more air, and lets more low sun underneath. Lower shades better late in the day and traps more heat. In between sits the clearance a ceiling fan needs, which on a Florida patio does more for comfort than anything else you can hang — and which an attached pergola sometimes cannot fit under a low eave.
What each one actually costs you
Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 as its base line, and what we show is that figure plus or minus 10%. It does not split by attachment, because the difference is site-specific:
Attached adds
the ledger, the flashing and sealing detail, sometimes blocking or an engineered connection into the wall, and a conversation with a roofer if the tie-in touches the roof.
Attached saves
two posts and two footings.
Freestanding adds
those two posts and footings — and the line nobody puts on a comparison sheet, the utility run.

That last one is the real divergence. Lights and fans against the house are a few feet from an existing circuit. Out in the middle of the yard they are a trench, conduit, and often a dedicated circuit. Our estimator prices LED fixtures at $450 each; that number does not change with distance. Getting power to them does.
So the honest summary is that the two layouts cost roughly the same in structure and separate in two items most quotes bury: wall detailing on one side, trenching on the other.
What changes an aluminum pergola's price
walks through the rest, and
the cost estimator
will put a range on your own version.
The layout most Florida houses end up with
Self-supporting, tucked under the eave. Four posts on their own footings, the beam set a few inches clear of the fascia, with a trim closure if you want the line to read clean from the yard.

It looks attached and behaves freestanding: no penetrations through the wall, no ledger to engineer, no roof warranty to argue about. Roof water still has to be handled, but it lands where you planned for it instead of onto a structure bolted into the wall it runs off.
It costs two more posts and two more footings than a true attached pergola. On most projects that is the cheapest problem on the list.

It stops working when the eave is low enough that the beam cannot fit under it and still clear the door head. At that point you are choosing between a true attached structure at the only height that fits, or moving off the house entirely — which is exactly the decision this article started with.
If screens might come later
An attached pergola gives you three sides to screen, because the house is the fourth. A freestanding one needs four, plus a header detail at the top of that fourth side.

Decide it now even if you build the screens later. The post spacing and beam depth a screen track needs are cheap to build in and expensive to retrofit. If a full enclosure is what you are really after,
what a pool screen enclosure costs in Florida
covers that route instead.
Beside a pool, two constraints get added

Footings cannot land on pool plumbing or the equipment runs, which narrows where a freestanding structure can go on a yard that already has a pool in it. And if there is an existing screen enclosure, the pergola lives either inside it, which the enclosure height rarely allows, or outside it, which changes the layout.
Both are workable when they come up before the layout is drawn.
Eight features worth planning together
goes through the rest of the pool-adjacent list.

blog.alt: Dark-framed pergola beside a kidney-shaped backyard pool, with overhead power lines crossing above the yard and a wooden louvered privacy screen and a bench underneath it.

children.text: How to settle it this weekend
Sit where you actually sit. Not where the pergola would look best from the kitchen window.
Measure from the patio to the top of the slider, and from the patio to the underside of the soffit. Write both down.
Stake the four post positions you would want and find out what is underneath them.
Watch the roof edge during the next afternoon storm and see where the water lands.
Then call about setbacks and, if you have one, the HOA.

A designer does all five on a site visit anyway. Doing them first changes what that visit is about: you arrive choosing between two layouts that both work, instead of being told which one does not. The rest of the pre-construction list is in
seven decisions to make before construction starts
How we build them — spans, footings, finishes and the attachment detail itself — is on the
aluminum pergola construction
page, and a
project estimate
starts with that site walk rather than with a number.

faq.answer: Not reliably. You save two posts and two footings, and you add a ledger, a flashing detail and sometimes an engineered connection into the wall. Our estimator carries a pergola at $8,500 as its base line and shows a range of plus or minus 10%; the attachment difference is site-specific and never appears as its own number.
faq.question: Is an attached pergola cheaper than a freestanding one?

faq.answer: No. It needs something structural to bolt through: block, a tie beam, studs or a band. Fascia board, stucco over foam trim, and a truss overhang with no continuous member at the height you want cannot carry one. On a structure this light the load that governs is wind trying to lift it, not weight pressing down.
faq.question: Can a pergola be attached to any wall?

faq.answer: Freestanding, when shade is the point. An open top only shades while the sun is high, and an attached pergola's rafters have to run perpendicular to the wall. A freestanding one can be turned against the worst afternoon sun. If the space faces west, the fix is the roof type rather than the layout.
faq.question: Which layout gives better shade?

faq.answer: Yes, and it is what most Florida houses end up with: a self-supporting structure tucked under the eave, four posts on their own footings, the beam set clear of the fascia. It reads attached from the yard and never penetrates the wall. It costs two more posts and footings than a true attached pergola.
faq.question: Is there a middle option between the two?

faq.answer: Both layouts are structures and both go through permitting and inspection. What varies is the county process and where each one is allowed to sit relative to setbacks. Have the work permitted and inspected under a licensed contractor's license, and confirm that license yourself on the state's public register.
faq.question: Does a freestanding pergola still need a permit?

children.text: The changes you actually see are the vertical ones: the waterline tile, the coping edge, and whatever stands up behind the water. The interior finish is usually the largest single line in a pool remodel and the one you notice least from the deck, because at standing height you are looking at reflected sky rather than at plaster.

That is not an argument for skipping the finish. It cannot be deferred once the pool is drained, and it sets the color of the water in every wide shot of the yard. It is an argument for sorting your list by what changes the view from the kitchen window and what only changes the drone photo. The ten below are sorted that way.
First, how to read anyone's before-and-after pair
Most before-and-after sets are partly a remodel and partly a photography difference. Three patterns account for nearly all of it:
Different time of day.
The before is shot at midday with hard shadows and a flat sky. The after is shot at dusk with the lights on. That alone will carry a pair.
Different height and lens.
The before is a phone held at chest height, close in, so the pool looks stretched and cramped. The after is a drone, stepped back, where every deck looks generous.
Different condition.
The before has a dirty waterline, a limp cover and a hose across the deck. The after has a wet deck, clean water and furniture that was placed that morning.

None of that is dishonest, but none of it is the remodel either. Ask for one pair taken from the same spot, at the same height, at the same time of day. Whatever difference survives is what you are buying. Apply the same test to
our own project gallery
: the photos worth learning from are the ones shot from where somebody would actually be standing.
The rule: rank by what stands up in your sightline

Standing on a deck, you see the water at a grazing angle, so most of what reaches you is reflection. Vertical surfaces reach you at full value: the tile band, the face of the coping, a raised wall, the screen frame, the house behind. Horizontal surfaces close to your feet — the deck — reach you at something in between, but they cover more area than anything else in the view.
So the honest ranking is not by cost. It is by how much of a change is standing up in front of you.

celdas: What you see standing on the deck
Where it lands in the budget
High. It frames the water at the line the eye tracks
High. It draws the whole outline of the pool
High. Largest area in the view
Large. The material sets the rate
High. Often the only thing standing up
High. Elevation is the thing you see
Medium. Changes the shape of the water
High. It decides whether there is room to sit
Large. The area sets the total
Low at eye level, high from above or at distance
Nothing by day, everything after dark
What you take away or screen
High, and the cheapest item on the list

children.text: The four you see first
1. The waterline tile band
The tile band is the single most reliable tell of a pool's age. Two things date it: the pattern, and the chalky calcium line sitting on top of it that no amount of brushing takes off.

It is also a small area. A band of tile is a narrow strip around a perimeter, which is why it delivers more visible change per dollar than anything else in a remodel. The decision worth making deliberately is height: a deeper band reads as a border and makes the pool look intentional, a thin one reads as trim. Whichever you choose, it is the element people photograph without meaning to, because it is exactly where the eye lands.
2. The coping
Coping is the edge you walk on and the line that draws the pool's shape. A worn bullnose concrete edge with chipped corners is what makes an otherwise sound pool look tired.

Two properties do the work, and only one of them usually gets discussed. The profile sets how sharp the outline reads. The overhang sets the shadow line under it, and that shadow is what separates the deck from the water in any photo taken in sunlight — a pool with a crisp line under the coping looks newer than the same pool without one. Neither the tile nor the finish compensates for an edge that is wrong.
3. The deck surface

The deck is the largest surface in almost every view of the pool, which makes it the biggest single lever on the after photo — and the biggest budget line that scales with area rather than with taste. Our estimator prices decking at $12 per square foot for concrete, $22 for pavers and $35 for travertine.

One note is worth more than the material choice: resist matching the house. A deck close in tone to the wall behind it gives the eye nothing to separate, and the result photographs as one flat field. Deliberate contrast is what gives a finished yard its depth — and unlike area, tone costs nothing to get right.
4. Whatever stands up behind the water

Most old pools have nothing vertical in the frame except the house and a fence. Adding one element that stands up — a rendered wall with scuppers, a raised planter, a fire feature, a pergola — changes the photo more than any surface swap, because it gives the eye something at full height to read.

It also adds movement and sound, which is the part that does not show up in any photograph and is the reason people keep sitting outside. The scope jump depends entirely on which one you pick: our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500, and a raised spa has its own line below. A rendered wall is priced by what it is built from and what it is founded on, which is why it belongs in the site conversation rather than in a table.

blog.alt: Rectangular pool with three spillway scuppers set into a rendered wall, a fire bowl on the deck and bougainvillea behind it.

children.text: The three that change the shape of what you are looking at
5. A raised spa instead of a flush one

A spa set flush with the deck disappears from every photo taken at standing height. Raised, it becomes the second thing you see after the water, and the spillway edge gives the pool a moving line. The difference in our estimator is $12,000 integrated against $18,000 with a spillway — the same appliance, a different object in the yard.
6. A tanning ledge or a wider entry

A ledge changes the outline of the water, which is the shape your eye actually reads. It also changes where people sit, which changes how the yard looks when it is in use rather than staged. This is structural work — the shell gets cut and formed — so it belongs in the scope from the start, not in a second visit.

blog.alt: Pool with an attached spa and travertine coping, two lounge chairs standing in the shallow water at the edge and patio furniture under the lanai behind.

children.text: 7. How much deck there is, not what it is made of

This is the one item on the list that changes the after photo without anything in it looking different. A pool ringed by an even walkway reads as a corridor in every frame, because there is nowhere in the picture for a person to be. Widen one side enough for a table or a pair of loungers and the same water, the same coping and the same surface read as a room.

So walk the footprint with a tape before anyone quotes a surface: area drives the deck budget far more than material does, and it also decides whether the finished yard has anywhere to sit. Which side to widen is a sun-and-use question rather than a visual one, and it is worked through in
the decisions that make an old pool feel new
The three nobody puts on the list
8. The interior finish

The finish is the largest visual change from above and from the far end of the yard, and the smallest one from three feet away. That is not a reason to spend less on it. It is the item that sets how many years you get before the pool comes offline again, and our estimator prices a pebble finish at 1.15 times plaster and a premium finish at 1.35 times.

It is a reason to stop treating the color sample as the centerpiece of the design meeting. Pick it for service life first. Whatever color you land on, the water will read as sky from where you stand and as the finish from the drone.

blog.alt: Aerial view of a house and pool ringed by palms, with a daybed under the porch, an outdoor kitchen beneath a metal roof and a red cornhole board on the lawn.

children.text: 9. Light

A good part of what sells an after photo is shot after dark, and none of it is possible without fixtures. A pool light is not a lamp — it is a niche in the shell wall with conduit behind it — so the moment to add one is while the shell is open. Our estimator prices pool LEDs at $450 per fixture.

The visual logic is simple. One light centered in a pool produces a glowing rectangle. Several, plus anything lighting the vertical surfaces behind the water, produces a yard with depth. One rule for the night photo: the light should hit what stands up, not only the water.
10. What you take away

The cheapest change on this list is deleting things from the sightline. The equipment pad visible from the patio door. The white ladder and handrail on a pool that no longer needs them. The chain-link line into the neighbor's yard. The cleaner hose. The hose reel.

Screening the yard is where landscape spending earns its keep on the visual side: our estimator prices landscaping at $8,000, and a hedge that hides a pad and a fence line does more for the view than the same money spent on a surface upgrade. Much of what makes a finished backyard look finished is the absence of things, and that is the part no idea list covers because there is nothing to photograph.
The order these have to happen in
Several of these lock each other: the tile band goes in while the shell is drained, and a light niche needs the shell wall open and the deck out for the conduit behind it.
That sequencing is a different axis from this one, and it is worked through in
what belongs in the scope while the pool is open
. Where the line sits between a surface job and a structural one is covered in
resurfacing versus a full renovation
, and the wider list of decisions — including the ones that change how the pool runs rather than how it looks — is in
the decisions that make an old pool feel new

One figure worth carrying into that conversation: our estimator prices a remodel at 82% of what the same work would cost as new construction, and shows every figure at plus or minus 10%. If your visual wish list has grown to a new spa, a new ledge, a full deck replacement and a raised wall, you are approaching new-build spending while keeping the one thing a remodel cannot change — the shape of the hole and where it sits in the yard. What that trade-off is worth is the subject of
what actually changes a remodel's scope
How to brief this so you get what you pictured
Ask for the design conversation in the order of this article rather than in the order of the quote:
What stands up.
Wall, spa elevation, pergola, planting. Decide the vertical elements first, because everything else is built around them.
The outline.
Coping profile, overhang, deck footprint and where the shape widens.
The edges.
Tile band height and pattern, coping material.
The fields.
Deck surface, interior finish.
The dark.
Light placement, on the water and on what stands up.
The subtraction.
Pad, rails, fence line, hose runs.

Then ask for one thing at the end: a photograph from the spot you stand in most often — usually the patio door — and a sketch or render from that same spot. Not the drone view. If the design does not work from the doorway, it does not matter how it looks from forty feet up, because that is not where you will ever be standing.
Our own scope on a
complete pool remodel
is organized the same way, and the
pool cost estimator
uses the figures quoted throughout this article if you want to test a budget before anyone visits. A
project estimate
starts in the yard, at the doorway, looking at the same view you do.

faq.answer: The waterline tile and the coping, taken together. They sit at the edge of the water where the eye goes first, they draw the entire outline of the pool, and their area is small compared with the deck. Neither happens with the pool full and running, so both belong inside the remodel rather than after it.
faq.question: Which single change makes the biggest visible difference for the money?

faq.answer: It changes how deep the water reads and what it reflects, but mostly from above or from a distance. Standing on the deck you are looking at reflected sky either way. Choose the finish for how many years it buys before the next drain and chip — our estimator prices pebble at 1.15 times plaster and a premium finish at 1.35 times — and for color second.
faq.question: Does a darker interior finish make the water look better?

faq.answer: Matching usually reads flat, because the deck is the largest surface in almost every view of the pool and a close match gives the eye nothing to separate. Area drives the cost far more than material does: our estimator prices decking at $12 per square foot for concrete, $22 for pavers and $35 for travertine.
faq.question: Should a new pool deck match the house?

faq.answer: Ask for the pair shot from the same position, at the same height, at the same time of day, with the water in the same state. Whatever difference survives that is the remodel. Whatever disappears was the camera.
faq.question: How do I tell a real before-and-after from a better photograph?

faq.answer: What drives the review is structure, deck area, electrical and plumbing rather than a like-for-like surface swap, and exactly where that line sits is set by the county building department reviewing your job. The practical rule holds everywhere: settle the whole list before the file goes in, because scope added after a permit is issued goes back through review as a revision.
faq.question: Do cosmetic changes need the same permitting as structural ones?

children.text: Pool projects rarely go wrong during construction. They go wrong in the two weeks before it, when decisions get deferred because nobody realizes they are about to become permanent.

Once the excavator is on site, the shape of the hole, where the equipment lives and how water leaves your yard are all settled. This is the list worth working through first, ordered roughly by how expensive each one is to change afterwards.
The three that are genuinely hard to undo
If you read nothing else, settle these:
Where the pool sits.
It drives setbacks, the equipment run, drainage and the enclosure footprint.
Whether there is a spa.
A spa shares structure with the pool. Adding one later means cutting into a finished shell.
Whether a screen enclosure is coming.
The deck has to be built to carry it, whether or not it goes up on day one.
Everything else on this list is easier to revisit. These three are not.
1. Where the pool actually goes
Setbacks decide what is legal. Sun, sightlines and the house decide what is pleasant.

A pool pushed to the rear setback maximizes deck between the house and the water, which is usually where people actually sit. A pool close to the house shortens the plumbing run and keeps the kids in view from the kitchen. Both are defensible; they are different houses to live in.
Worth checking before you commit: where the afternoon sun lands in summer, and what the neighbors see.
2. Spa or no spa

Decide now. An integrated spa shares a wall with the pool; a spillover spa sits raised and returns water over a weir. Both are structural, and both are part of the shell that gets formed and poured once.
The relevant costs are in
what a custom pool really costs
— but the reason it belongs on this list is not the money, it is that the window closes.
3. Screen enclosure, now or never cheaply
You do not have to build the enclosure with the pool. You do have to decide whether one is coming, because the deck carries it.

If an enclosure is likely within a few years, building the deck to take it costs very little now and saves cutting a finished deck later. If it is definitely not coming, you can spend that deck budget on surface instead. What is expensive is not deciding — see
pool screen enclosures
for what the structure needs.

blog.alt: Pool with arcing water spouts and a covered seating area, with a lake and palms beyond the boundary.

children.text: 4. How equipment gets to the back yard

This one surprises people. If a mini-excavator cannot physically reach your yard — a narrow side gate, a neighbor's wall, a mature tree in the only route — the work happens by hand or by crane, and the whole project carries a surcharge.

Walk the route yourself before anyone quotes. Measure the narrowest point. If it is tight, say so early: it changes the number, and a builder who discovers it on day one has to change the number anyway.
5. What is under the ground
Rock, a high water table and old fill all change excavation. None of them are visible from the surface, and all of them are cheaper to find out about before the contract than during the dig.
6. Where the water goes
Florida rain arrives fast and in quantity. A new pool and a new deck replace absorbent yard with hard surface, which has to drain somewhere that is not your slab or your neighbor's.
Drainage is designed alongside the deck, not added to it. If you are also planning
landscaping
, plan the two together — the grading serves both.
7. The equipment pad
Pumps and heaters need somewhere to live: reachable for service, close enough to keep the plumbing run short, and far enough from bedroom windows that nobody minds the noise.
The default is "wherever there is space down the side of the house". It is worth five minutes of thought, because moving it later means re-running plumbing and electrical.
8. Heating, and what it costs to run
Heating decides how many months a year the pool is usable, which for most families decides whether it gets used at all.
It also changes the plumbing and the electrical service, so it belongs before the shell, not after. The choice between a heat pump and gas is a running-cost question more than a purchase question.
9. Sanitation

A salt system and traditional chlorine end up in the same chemistry; they differ in how you handle it day to day and in what the water feels like. Salt also has implications for the materials around the pool, which is a reason to decide it alongside the deck rather than after.

blog.alt: Pool with in-water loungers and an aluminium pergola attached to the house, with newly laid turf around the deck.

children.text: 10. Lighting, and how many

Pool lights are run before the shell is finished. The number is a decision, not a detail: too few leaves dark water at the ends, and the usual mistake is one light in a pool long enough to need three.
Think about the deck and the yard at the same time — the pool is rarely the only thing you want lit after dark.
11. What else is coming to this yard
An
outdoor kitchen
, a
pergola
or a
deck extension
are all cheaper built while the crews, the access and the slab work are already on site.
You do not have to build them now. You do want to know where they go, so the pool and the deck leave room and the sleeves and conduit go in while the ground is open.
12. When you actually want to swim in it

Work backwards. A Florida pool project runs through permitting, excavation, steel, plumbing, shell, tile and deck, finish and startup — with inspections between stages that have to pass before the next begins.
That sequence, and what tends to move it, is covered in
the pool construction timeline
. The planning point is simply that a target date set without it is a wish.

blog.alt: Rectangular pool with a raised spa and water spouts, set in a herringbone travertine deck.

children.text: A short pre-excavation checklist
Before anything is dug, you should be able to answer:
Where the pool sits, and why there rather than three feet over.
Spa: yes or no.
Screen enclosure: coming, possibly coming, or never.
The narrowest point on the access route, measured.
Where stormwater goes.
Where the equipment pad is, and what it will be heard from.
Heating: yes or no, and which kind.
Lights: how many.
What else is coming to this yard, and roughly where.
If any of those is still "we will figure it out", figure it out now. Every one of them is cheap today and expensive once the ground is open.
When you have answers, a site visit is what turns them into a plan — see
custom pool and spa construction

faq.answer: Before the survey goes to the county. Placement drives the setbacks, the equipment run, the drainage plan and the screen enclosure footprint, so moving it after submission usually means resubmitting rather than adjusting.
faq.question: How early does the pool location have to be final?

faq.answer: Yes, but the deck has to have been poured to carry it. An enclosure is anchored into the deck, and a deck that was not designed for those loads either limits what can be built or needs cutting and reworking. Deciding early costs nothing; deciding late costs deck.
faq.question: Can I add a screen enclosure later?

faq.answer: Inspections and weather far more often than construction itself. The build is a sequence of stages separated by inspections, and each one has to pass before the next begins, so a single failed inspection moves everything behind it.
faq.question: What usually delays a Florida pool project?

faq.answer: Yes, because heating changes the plumbing and the electrical service, not just the equipment pad. Adding it later means opening up runs that are already buried.
faq.question: Do I need to decide on heating before the shell is built?

children.text: Three choices decide whether a Florida outdoor kitchen still looks right in year ten: a frame that cannot rot or corrode, which means concrete block, marine-grade polymer or welded aluminum; hardware and fasteners in 316 stainless anywhere near salt air or a saltwater pool; and a countertop in UV-stable natural stone or porcelain, which means granite, quartzite or a sintered slab, and not engineered quartz.

The order matters more than the list. Almost everyone spends their design time on the countertop, which is the part least likely to fail, and almost no time on the frame and the screws, which are the parts that do. Both are buried inside the island. Replacing either one means taking off the countertop that was chosen so carefully, which is why the cheapest line on the quote is usually the line that decides the expensive repair.
Failure runs from the inside out
Outdoor kitchens here do not fail the way people picture. Nothing dramatic happens to the stone. What happens is a sequence, and it runs in roughly this order:
Fasteners, hinges and drawer slides.
The smallest parts and the first to go. A door does not fail because the panel corroded; it fails because the hinge did, and then the panel hangs crooked and water gets behind it.
The frame.
Rot in wood, rust at the cut edges of galvanized steel studs. Invisible until a door will not line up or the countertop develops a dip, at which point the stone has to come off to reach it.
Mortar, grout and sealant joints.
Hairline cracks at corners, efflorescence blooming through stucco, a countertop-to-cabinet joint that opens up. Cosmetic first, a water path second.
The countertop.
Last, and usually cosmetic even then: a stain, an etched patch, a chip on an unsupported edge.
Budgets tend to run in the exact opposite direction. If you are deciding where an extra thousand dollars goes, it does more for you in hardware and framing than in a nicer slab.
One island, three exposure zones

A single kitchen run almost never lives in one climate. Under a solid roof, set back from the edge, the conditions are close to indoors. The end of the same island that pokes past the roof line gets direct rain. The end facing west gets afternoon sun on the stone and the door fronts every day of the year, and if there is a pool or the coast nearby, it gets the salt too.

Most kitchens are specified as though the whole run were the sheltered part. That is why you see an island where one end still looks new and the other has chalked door fronts and a faded countertop, on the same job, installed on the same day.
The rule is simple and it costs almost nothing to follow:
spec the entire run for its worst zone.

Mixing grades along one island saves a small amount of money and guarantees a visible line between the two halves within a few seasons. Where the island sits relative to the roof line, and therefore how many zones it has to survive, is settled in the
outdoor kitchen layout guide
— and it is worth settling before you choose a single material.

blog.alt: Outdoor kitchen under a palm-thatch roof with a ceiling fan: a dark countertop over a slatted wood island, a built-in grill and vent hood against a tropical leaf-patterned wall, an under-counter stainless refrigerator and a pale tile floor.

children.text: The frame you will never see again
This is the structure inside the island: the thing the doors hang on and the countertop sits on. Once it is clad and topped, you are not looking at it again without demolition.

celdas: Nothing in it can rot or rust; the natural base for stone or stucco veneer
Heavy. Needs a proper slab or footing under it, and it is permanent — no moving it later
Will not rot, rust or absorb water; the cabinet is the finish, so there is nothing to refinish
Moves with heat, so the system has to be engineered for that; ask where the countertop load actually lands
Light, non-corroding, straightforward to clad in any finish
Every fastener into it must be compatible metal; cut ends and welds need coating
Every cut end is bare steel. In this climate that is where it starts
Fast, cheap, familiar to any carpenter
Humidity that never fully dries, termites, and a cement board skin that hides all of it until it is bad

children.text: Concrete block is the default when the kitchen is staying put forever and the finish is stone, tile or stucco. It is the most forgiving structure we build here and the least forgiving to change your mind about.

Marine-grade polymer is the one homeowners are most skeptical of and most often end up happy with, because the cabinet material and the finish are the same thing: there is no coating to fail, no substrate to reach. The question to ask a builder is a structural one, not a cosmetic one — whether the stone is carried by the cabinets themselves or by a separate frame behind them.
Welded aluminum sits between the two, and it is the right answer when the kitchen has to be light, on a raised deck or a screened enclosure slab rather than on grade.

Wood framing with cement board over it is extremely common, and it is the construction we most often find quietly failing when we open up an island during a remodel. Cement board is not what rots. The frame behind it is.
Salt does most of the work, and it does it to hardware

Stainless steel is not one material. The grade that matters outdoors here is the difference between 304 and 316: 316 contains molybdenum, and that is what gives it its resistance to chlorides. Chloride is what salt air and salt water deliver.
Two things follow from that, and both get missed.
The upgrade belongs on the parts nobody looks at.

It is common to see 316 door panels hung on 304 hinges, driven with whatever screws came in the box. The panel is the largest and cheapest part to protect; the hinge, the slide, the bracket and the screw are the ones whose failure takes the assembly with them.
Do not mix metals in a wet, salty joint.

A plain steel screw into an aluminum frame, or a random fastener into a stainless door frame, sets up galvanic corrosion at exactly the point that stays wet longest. Fasteners should match what they are going into.

Even good stainless discolors near the coast. Surface staining on 304 in marine air is normal and it is cosmetic, not structural, as long as the steel underneath is sound. It responds to washing. Anything that will be near salt should be planned as something you rinse occasionally rather than something you never touch.

And a saltwater pool counts. A salt chlorination system puts chloride in the water, and splash carries it to whatever is within range. A kitchen within splash range of a salt pool is closer to a coastal environment than an owner inland in Ocala expects.

blog.alt: Covered lanai outdoor kitchen: a built-in stainless grill and a small stainless access door set into a white stucco base under a dark countertop, an under-counter stainless unit at the end of the run, and a travertine floor.

children.text: Two more hardware details worth naming in the spec: the cabinet interiors need to drain and breathe, because a sealed box under a countertop in this humidity is a condensation trap; and any enclosure around a gas appliance needs the ventilation the appliance requires, which is a safety requirement rather than a preference. What the appliances demand of the island is covered in
what to run before construction
, and it needs to be settled before the frame is built, not after.
Countertops: what survives the sun

celdas: Natural stone, stable under ultraviolet light, hard enough to take real use
Sealing on a schedule; dark colors get genuinely hot in direct sun
Natural stone, harder than granite, holds up to acid better than marble
Fewer slabs available; verify it is actually quartzite and not a soft stone sold as one
Non-porous, UV-stable, will not stain, consistent color across the run
Edges and overhangs need full support underneath; fabrication is specialized
Any shape or edge you want, integral color, no seams where you do not want them
Hairline cracking is inherent; needs sealing and periodic re-sealing
Inexpensive, repairable a piece at a time
The grout is the whole story; it is the maintenance and the failure point
Look right in a lot of Florida architecture
Soft and acid-sensitive: citrus, wine and cleaners etch it. Better on the floor than the counter

children.text: Quartz and quartzite are not the same material
This costs people real money, and the names are one letter apart.

Quartzite is natural stone, quarried and cut. Engineered quartz is quartz aggregate bound together in a polymer resin. The resin is the problem: it is not stable under ultraviolet light, and manufacturers know it, which is why outdoor installation is commonly excluded from the warranty.

That exclusion is the most reliable piece of information in the entire category. Read it before you fall in love with a slab, and read it even if the kitchen is going under a roof, because reflected light reaches further under a lanai than people assume and the wording rarely makes an exception for it.
Dark stone, west-facing

Color choice is not only aesthetic here. A dark countertop on the sunny end of a run can be too hot to rest your hand on for most of the afternoon — not a durability failure, just a counter you stop using during the hours you built it for. If the island is exposed and facing west, that is an argument for a lighter surface on that section, or for getting a roof over it.
Cladding is a finish, not a shell

Stone veneer, stucco, tile, porcelain panel, composite boards: these are how the island looks, not how it stays dry. Water gets behind every one of them eventually. What keeps the kitchen sound is the frame behind and the drainage under.

Two failure modes recur. Efflorescence — white mineral bloom pushing through stucco or grout — means water is moving through the assembly and picking up salts on the way. And hairline cracks appear at outside corners first, because that is where movement concentrates.
Neither is fatal. Both are information, and both are much cheaper to act on early than to explain away.

blog.alt: L-shaped outdoor kitchen clad in white stacked stone under a white louvered roof with a ceiling fan, with a built-in stainless grill and stainless doors and drawers, and a pond with tile-roofed houses behind.

children.text: The joints leak before the materials fail
Almost every water problem we open up starts at a joint rather than in the middle of a material:
The countertop-to-cabinet joint, where sealant was never renewed.
The sink cutout, where the underside of the stone was never sealed.
The grill cutout, where the appliance flange does not quite land on flat stone.
The back edge, where the island meets a house wall and nobody detailed the transition.
Sealant is a maintenance item, not a permanent product. Knowing that at handover — which joints, how often — is worth more than any single upgrade on this page.
What is under the island matters too

The island sits on something, and that surface has to move water away from it. Travertine, paver and concrete decks all work; what matters is that the slope runs away from the kitchen and that there is no low spot where the base of the island sits in standing water after every storm.

If the kitchen is going on a deck rather than on grade, the structure below has to carry the load of masonry, stone and appliances, which is a different calculation than the one for furniture. That gets planned at the framing stage on the
custom deck
side, not after the island is drawn.
What this does to the budget

Our estimator carries a full outdoor kitchen at $25,000, and what it shows anyone is a range of roughly ten percent either side of that. It is a starting configuration, not a spec sheet, and the materials on this page are most of what moves a real project away from it.

The useful thing to understand is which direction each choice pushes. Moving from wood framing to block or polymer is a modest change in the total. Moving from 304 to 316 hardware is smaller still. Moving from granite to a large-format sintered slab, or adding a second run and a bar overhang, moves it much more. The corrosion decisions are cheap; the size and stone decisions are not. That is almost exactly the opposite of how people rank them going in.
What drives the rest of the number, line by line, is in
what an outdoor kitchen actually costs in Florida
How to write the spec
Six lines, handed to whoever is quoting:
Frame material, named: block, marine-grade polymer or welded aluminum.
Stainless grade for doors, drawers
and
the hardware behind them, stated separately.
Fastener metal, matched to what it goes into.
Countertop material and finish, with the warranty checked for outdoor use.
How the cabinet interiors drain and vent, and what the appliance manufacturer requires.
Which joints are sealed, and how often they need renewing.
If a quote answers all six, you can compare it to another quote. If it says "stainless steel cabinets, granite top," you are comparing two numbers that describe different kitchens.
Finished examples of these assemblies, on real jobs, are in the
project gallery
, and the way we build them is on the
custom outdoor kitchens
page. If you want the material decisions made against your actual site — how far the roof reaches, where the salt comes from, what the deck can carry — that starts with a
site visit and estimate
rather than a slab sample.

faq.answer: Granite, quartzite and porcelain or sintered slab all hold up to sun and rain here. The choice between them is about edges, overhangs and heat rather than durability. Engineered quartz is the one to rule out, because the resin binding it is not stable under ultraviolet light.
faq.question: What is the best countertop material for an outdoor kitchen in Florida?

faq.answer: Read the manufacturer's warranty before deciding. Most exclude outdoor installation, and a covered lanai does not always count as indoors in that wording. Reflected light and afternoon sun reach further under a roof than people expect, and the exclusion usually applies to the whole slab regardless.
faq.question: Can I use engineered quartz outdoors if it is under a roof?

faq.answer: Near the coast or beside a saltwater pool, yes, and it is worth it specifically on the parts nobody looks at: hinges, drawer slides, screws and brackets. On an inland site with a chlorine pool, 304 on doors with better hardware behind them is a reasonable place to spend less.
faq.question: Is 316 stainless worth the upgrade over 304?

faq.answer: It does, and it surprises people who are nowhere near the ocean. A salt chlorination system puts chloride into the water, and splash and spray carry it onto anything close by. Treat a kitchen within splash range of a salt pool the way you would treat a coastal site.
faq.question: Does a saltwater pool affect the materials I should choose?

faq.answer: Wood framing behind cement board is common and it is the construction we most often find failing during a remodel. The board is not what rots. If a wood frame is already there and sound, it can be clad and kept, but it is not what we would build new in this climate.

children.text: Building a pool in Gainesville or Ocala is the same project as building one in Fort Lauderdale for most of its length. The parts that differ are the parts that move money and dates, and there are four: what is under the yard, where the fill water comes from, how many months the pool is warm enough to use, and which office reviews the permit.
None of the four changes how a pool is designed. All four change what it costs and how long it takes, and all four are cheaper to settle before the contract than during the dig.
The decisions that apply anywhere in the state — siting, drainage, the equipment pad, lighting, when you actually want to swim — are covered in
12 decisions to make before excavation
. This article is only the part that changes once you are north of Orlando.
The four, in the order they bite
Rock.
Limestone close to the surface, and not evenly across the lot.
Well water.
What is in the fill water ends up on the finish.
Season.
A shorter unheated swim window changes the heating decision, not just the budget line.
Jurisdiction.
City or county, decided by a line on a map rather than by your address.
Trees and access come after those, because in this part of the state they are usually the same problem.
1. The ground is limestone, and it is not always deep

Alachua and Marion County sit on a limestone belt. That is why the springs are here, why sinkhole activity is a known feature of the region, and why the depth to rock in a back yard is a real question rather than a formality.

The part homeowners underestimate is that rock does not arrive evenly. Depth to rock can change across a single back yard, so one end of the hole finds it and the other does not. That matters because a pool is not a hole of uniform depth — the deep end, the spa footing and the plumbing trenches all reach lower than the shallow end, so rock can affect part of the excavation and leave the rest alone. It also means a test boring tells you about the spot it was taken in, not about the lot.

When rock does show up, the cost is not extra hours with the same machine. It is a different method: heavier equipment, hammering, and hauling out material that a standard dig would have pushed aside. That is why it is priced as a surcharge on the project rather than as a line item.

blog.alt: Raised spa with bubblers running, clad in dark blue mosaic tile, in a rectangular pool whose white coping sits flush with the surrounding lawn.

children.text: What to settle before you sign
Ask one question and listen carefully to the answer:
is rock priced in this contract, or is it a change order?

Both answers are legitimate. A builder who has priced it is carrying the risk and the number reflects that. A builder who treats it as a change order is quoting you a lower figure that may not survive the excavation. What is not legitimate is a contract that is silent, because silence resolves in the builder's favor at the worst possible moment — when the machine is already in the yard.
If you are comparing two quotes and one is noticeably cheaper, this is the first place to look. The other places are in
what a custom pool really costs
2. Outside the city, the water comes from a well
Much of Alachua and Marion County is on private well and septic. That changes two things about a pool, and neither is obvious from a rendering.
Iron, and why it shows up once the pool is already full
Water from the Floridan aquifer is hard — high in dissolved calcium, which is what limestone is made of — and in many wells it also carries iron. Both matter at exactly one moment: the first fill.

A pool holds tens of thousands of gallons, and on a well that whole volume comes out of the ground in one draw — the largest the well will ever be asked for. If that water carries iron, the iron goes in with it and does not stay dissolved. It comes out of solution on the walls and floor as brown or rust-colored staining, early rather than late, and once it has set into a fresh interior finish it is not something you scrub off. Hard water has the opposite failure mode: scale, which builds slowly and shows first at the waterline.

The fix is cheap and has to happen before the water goes in — test the well, pre-filter the fill, and treat the water from the first day rather than from the first complaint. Finish choice buys a margin, not an exemption: our estimator prices a pebble interior at 1.15 times plaster, and a textured surface hides minor discoloration that smooth plaster shows plainly. It does not stop iron from staining. That is dealt with in the fill or it is not dealt with.

None of that is a reason to avoid filling from a well. It is a reason to have the conversation before startup rather than after, because the same problem costs a filter before and a drain-and-refinish after.
The drainfield decides where the pool goes

On a septic lot, the drainfield is not a soft constraint. You cannot build a pool over it, you cannot deck over it, and you cannot drive an excavator across it — which means the drainfield often decides both where the pool sits and how the equipment reaches the back yard.

Two more things follow from it. Backwash from a sand filter has to go somewhere that is not the septic system, so where the water goes is a design question on these lots rather than an afterthought. And if the pool has to move to clear the field, that usually moves the deck, the equipment pad and the plumbing runs with it. That is a site-plan conversation, not a change you make later.

blog.alt: Three sheer-descent waterfalls falling from a raised tiled wall into a pool, with an aluminum pergola and lounge seating on the travertine deck to the left.

children.text: 3. Winter is real here, which changes the heating math

This is the difference people from further south are least prepared for. A pool in Broward County is comfortable for most of the year without help. A pool in Gainesville or Ocala is not — the unheated season is meaningfully shorter, and the months at the edges, when the air is pleasant and the water is not, are exactly when a back yard is most usable.

So heating here is not an upgrade that extends a long season. It is what determines whether you get spring and fall at all. Our estimator prices a heater at $4,500. What it does not price is the supply that heater needs, and that is where the North Florida difference sits:

celdas: Low running cost across a season, with no fuel to have delivered
Output falls as the air gets colder, which is precisely when you want it. Also confirm the electrical service can carry it
Heats on demand regardless of air temperature, so it suits weekend use
Natural gas service is not a given outside the city limits here, so gas often means propane, a tank and a delivery schedule
Almost nothing to run; pairs with a heat pump rather than replacing one
Needs unshaded roof area, which the tree canopy in both areas often does not allow

children.text: There is a second cold-weather item that belongs in the same conversation. When the temperature drops toward freezing, water sitting still in pool plumbing is a problem; water that keeps moving is not. Automated controls run the pump when that happens, without anyone waking up to do it. Our estimator prices automation at $3,500, and in this part of the state it is closer to protection than to convenience.
4. Your address decides who reviews the permit
A pool permit in Florida is issued by whoever has jurisdiction over the parcel. In this region that is one of four offices, and which one it is has nothing to do with what your mail says.

Plenty of homes with a Gainesville or Ocala address are in the unincorporated county. Plenty of subdivisions sit right at the line. The practical consequence is that submittal requirements, review queues and inspection scheduling are not the same from one to the next, so a timeline quoted before anyone has confirmed jurisdiction is a guess.
Two other things worth knowing here. The pool is not one permit — the shell, the electrical, the plumbing and any barrier or enclosure are separate reviews, and
what permits are required for pool construction in Florida

covers what a full set looks like. And our estimator prices permits and engineering at 9 percent of the pool and deck combined, which on a typical project is a four-figure line rather than a rounding error.

If you are in a newer subdivision, an HOA architectural review usually sits in front of all of that. The estimator prices that submittal at $1,500, and the thing to plan for is not the fee but the calendar: an HOA review happens before the permit application, not alongside it.
Trees and access, which are usually the same problem

Lots in this region tend to be larger than their South Florida equivalents, which sounds like it should make construction easier. It rarely does, because the constraint is never the size of the yard — it is the width of the gap between the house and the fence, and what is standing in it.

Live oaks are the usual complication. They are the reason the yard is worth building in, they are often exactly where the equipment needs to pass, and their root zones extend well beyond what the canopy suggests. Before you commit to a pool location, ask whether the trees you would need to remove are regulated where you are. In this part of the state that question has a real answer more often than homeowners expect, and the answer can move a pool several feet.

Access itself is priced. Our estimator applies an 8 percent surcharge for difficult access, and what counts as difficult is specific: a gate too narrow for the machine, a slope that has to be built up, a septic field that cannot be crossed, a tree that cannot come out. On rural Marion County properties the pinch point is often further out — a long driveway, a fence line, or the reach a concrete pump needs to get to the back of the parcel.
One thing that genuinely does get easier on a larger lot: the equipment pad and the future structures have room. If a
screen enclosure
is likely later — and under oak canopy, leaf load makes it more likely here than at the coast — its footings belong in the deck plan now.

blog.alt: Pool and spa on a travertine deck with two white loungers, seen from a covered lanai, with a lake and palms behind the fence.

children.text: What this does to the estimate
What sets the base price of a Florida pool — size, style, interior finish, deck, spa — is worked through in
what a custom pool really costs
. What belongs here is how the two North Florida surcharges attach to that base, because it is not where most people assume.
Rock excavation and difficult access are not priced against the excavation. In our
pool cost estimator

they multiply the project: the shell, the deck, the spa, the equipment, the outdoor features and the permit line, all of it. So the same rock costs more on a bigger job. A pool with a large travertine deck, an outdoor kitchen and landscaping carries the 12 percent on all of that, not on the hole — and because permits are themselves 9 percent of pool and deck, the surcharge lands on the permit line too.
On the estimator's own default configuration the shape is clear: ticking rock excavation and nothing else adds roughly
, and ticking difficult access as well puts the pair at about
, for a pool of identical design.

So the North Florida difference is not a different pool and not a different price per square foot. It is the same pool with two site conditions attached, and they are the two lines most likely to arrive later as a change order if nobody looked first. Every figure here comes from the same approved price table the estimator uses, and what it returns is a range of plus or minus 10 percent, not a quote.
Four questions to settle before you sign
Is rock priced in this contract, or is it a change order?
Get the answer in writing either way.
Has anyone tested the well water that will fill this pool?
Before startup, not after the first stain.
Which authority issues this permit, and has the HOA review started?
Both are calendar items, and they are sequential.
What is the route for equipment, and what has to move for it?
Trees, gates and the drainfield, specifically.
A builder who answers those four quickly is a builder who has worked in this region. If the answers are vague, the questions in
how to choose a pool builder in Florida
are the next thing to read.
We build across this region —
Gainesville
and
Ocala
Alachua County
and
Marion County
, and the rest of
North Florida
. How our
custom pool and spa construction
is sequenced, from site review through permitting to startup, is on the service page, and a
project estimate
starts with someone walking the yard — which, given everything above, is the only place it can start.

faq.answer: Often, yes. This part of the state sits on limestone that can be shallow, and shallow rock changes the excavation method rather than just the hours. Our estimator applies a 12 percent rock-excavation surcharge to the project, which on its own default configuration is about $11,000.
faq.question: Does rock really cost more to dig in Gainesville and Ocala?

faq.answer: Usually, but test the water first. Well water in this region is hard and can carry iron, and iron that goes into a pool on the first fill can stain a new interior finish within weeks. The fix is pre-filtering the fill and treating the water from day one, which is easy before startup and expensive afterward.
faq.question: Can I fill a new pool from my well?

faq.answer: It depends on whether the property is inside city limits or in the unincorporated county, not on the mailing address. A Gainesville or Ocala address can fall under either. Confirm which authority has jurisdiction before anyone promises you a start date, because the submittal and inspection process is not the same.
faq.question: Who issues the pool permit in Alachua or Marion County?

faq.answer: If you want to swim outside the warmest months, yes. This is not South Florida: the unheated season is shorter, and a heater is what decides whether the pool gets used in spring and fall. Our estimator prices a heater at $4,500, with the gas supply or electrical capacity it needs priced separately.

pool construction budget
goals and optimize
pool installation cost

factors, including excavation and decking. Custom features, such as lighting or spas, impact concrete pool cost. Experts recommend phased planning to balance upfront expenses with long-term maintenance savings.

Florida's unique subtropical climate, hurricane risks, and booming tourism industry make
commercial pool construction
distinct, demanding resilient designs that balance aesthetics with environmental challenges. High humidity accelerates wear on materials, while salt air near coasts causes
corrosion
issues. These factors elevate pool installation cost compared to other regions.

pool investment Florida
returns.

Salt air corrosion affects metal components, favoring
fiberglass pool cost
