children.text: A complete pool remodel is not measured in crew days. Most of its calendar is spent waiting — on a selection you have not made, on an inspection, on a cure, on equipment that was ordered late — and the number of those waits is fixed by your scope before anyone touches the pool. That is why two remodels that look identical on paper can run on completely different calendars, and why the question worth asking a builder is not how many weeks, but how many stops your scope contains and what starts each one.

Any finish date offered before demolition is a best case. That is not dishonest; it is what happens when you work on something that is already built and cannot be fully seen until it is opened. What you can get before you sign is the shape of the schedule.
If your scope is a single item — resurfacing and nothing else — the calendar looks different from the one described here.
Resurfacing versus a full renovation
draws that line. Everything below assumes a complete remodel: surface, tile, coping and at least one system.
A remodel is not a faster pool

Our estimator prices a remodel at 82% of what the same work would cost as new construction. The calendar does not scale the same way, and expecting it to is the most common way homeowners get surprised.

A new pool is built in one direction, in an empty hole, with nothing to work around. A remodel is fitted to what is already in the ground: old plumbing runs, a deck someone else poured, an equipment pad sized for equipment nobody makes any more. Fewer crew days, similar number of stops, plus one thing new construction never has to absorb — discovery.
The pool construction timeline
covers the new-build sequence; this article is about where the two diverge.
The three kinds of days
Every day on a remodel belongs to one of three categories, and they are not controlled by the same person.

celdas: Almost nothing. The trades take the time the work takes
Nobody in the room: reviews, inspections, cures, lead times
Scope decisions made before the job starts

children.text: In most complete remodels, crew days are the smallest of the three. That has a blunt implication: a bigger crew does not shorten a remodel. A builder who promises speed by promising manpower has misread their own schedule, because manpower does not shorten a plaster cure, an electrical inspection or a gas review.
The order it runs in
Remodels run in the same order every time. Knowing the order is what lets you see where your own scope inserts a stop, and which steps cannot be pulled forward no matter how motivated everybody is.

celdas: Getting the pool looked at, and drained first if the shell itself has to be judged
Selections are final and the drawings match them
The county's review queue, and the HOA board if there is one
The permit set is in hand and a crew is booked
How deep the demolition has to go
What the old surface was hiding
Rough inspections, which hold the job until they pass
The rough work has been signed off
The pad and the power are ready
When the equipment was ordered, not when it is installed
The finish crew's calendar; the surface goes on in one go, not in stages
Whether the final payment is still meaningful

children.text: Two of those rows are where remodels actually slip. Discovery, because it lands in the middle of the job rather than at the start, and what it finds can need its own review. And permit submission, because it sits downstream of your selections: a drawing set that no longer matches what you finally chose goes back out and waits again, which is a delay caused entirely before anyone picked up a hammer.
Where the stops come from

The work in your scope divides cleanly into two groups: work that touches a permitted system, and work that does not. The first group stops and waits for someone outside your builder's crew. The second does not.

celdas: Adds a review or inspection stop
The finish crew's sequence and the start-up procedure
Surface area, and whether anything structural changes
A rough inspection before anything gets covered
Electrical review, and the utility if service changes
Adding a spa to an existing pool
The same reviews a new shell gets: it is new construction attached to an old pool
Its own permit and its own footings
Not an inspection, but a stop
A board's meeting calendar, not yours

children.text: Which reviews apply, and in what order, is set by your county: the process in Alachua is not the process in Broward. What holds everywhere is that the work is permitted and inspected under the contractor's license, and that every line marked yes above is a point where the crew leaves the site until somebody else signs.
What permits are required for pool construction in Florida
shows what a full set looks like; a remodel pulls a subset of the same reviews, and which subset is decided entirely by what you choose to open.
The HOA line is the one people underestimate. Our estimator carries $1,500 for an HOA submission, and the money is the easy part — the calendar cost is a board that meets when it meets.

blog.alt: Aerial view of a backyard pool with a robotic cleaner on the floor, a daybed under the porch and an outdoor kitchen beneath a metal roof.

children.text: The stop with your name on it
Every selection you have not made is a stop, and it is the only category of delay you own outright. Before chip-out, these should all be decided and in the contract:
the interior finish and its color
waterline tile and coping
deck material and pattern, if the deck is in scope
light count and placement
equipment: heater or not, salt chlorination or not, automation or not
any spa work, which is the largest single scope decision in a remodel
The rule is simple and almost nobody follows it.
Chip-out is the deadline for selections, not the start of shopping for them.

Once the shell is open, every day spent deciding is a day the pool sits empty and the crew is on somebody else's job — and getting back onto a crew's calendar is its own wait, routinely longer than the decision that caused it.
Equipment is the selection whose clock starts at the order, not at the install. Our
pool cost estimator

prices a heater at $4,500, salt chlorination at $2,200 and automation at $3,500. What the prices do not show is that a remodel which adds any of them has to decide it at design, because the pad, the power and the plumbing get built around the choice. Which ones are worth adding is the subject of
what to upgrade while the pool is open
; the timeline argument is narrower — anything you add later means opening the same ground twice.

blog.alt: Spa running with its jets on beside the pool, with a grill and cart under the lanai and an orange hammock on the lawn.

children.text: The empty shell is a clock of its own

The moment the old surface is chipped out, the pool is empty, and an empty pool in Florida is a managed condition rather than a neutral one: groundwater sits high across much of the state, and a drained shell has water pressure on the outside and nothing pushing back on the inside. Managed is the operative word — the hydrostatic relief valve in the floor, dewatering when the site needs it, and above all keeping the window short. Keeping it short is a scheduling decision, which is why an open selection costs more after chip-out than it does before.

The practical consequence runs against instinct. It is better to delay the start of a remodel than to start it with three selections still open. Delaying costs you time with the pool you already have. Starting early costs you the same time with the pool out of service, and it moves the risk of every later delay into whatever season you land in.
Rain season, and everyone else's calendar
Season affects a remodel twice, in two unrelated ways.

The first is weather. Chip-out, a deck pour and the application of a new interior finish are all work that cannot be done wet. Rain does not cancel those days, it pushes them, and a pushed day pushes everything sequenced behind it.

The second is demand. Remodels cluster in the months before summer, because that is when people notice they want the pool back. The same seasonal wave books the finish crews and the deck crews, so the wait to get onto a schedule is longest exactly when everybody wants one. The practical move is to sign in the season before the season you want to swim in — a job that starts when everyone else's is ending gets crews that are not stacked three deep.
The job is not over when the water goes in

A new interior finish has a start-up procedure. The pool is filled without stopping, the water is balanced and brushed on a schedule, and some equipment stays off until the surface has cured — salt chlorination and heaters are commonly held back for a period the finish manufacturer sets, not the builder. Ask for that procedure in writing on the day the finish is applied. The first weeks of a new surface are when it is easiest to damage permanently, and it is usually the homeowner who does it.

The punch list is the other tail. It is the short list of things that are not right at the end, and it closes quickly on jobs where the final payment still means something and slowly where it does not.

blog.alt: Pool with a blue float in the water beside a marble deck, an outdoor shower on the house wall and a dining table under tree shadows.

children.text: Five questions that tell you whether there is a schedule
How many points does my scope have where the work stops and waits on somebody outside your crew?
Which single wait is the longest, and what starts its clock?
What has to be selected before chip-out, and what is the deadline for each one?
How many days will the pool sit empty, and how is the shell handled while it does?
If I sign a change order mid-job, what happens to my place in your schedule?

You are not checking the answers against a right answer. You are checking whether the builder has a schedule or an intention. A builder who can name the longest wait in your scope without looking anything up has run this before, and that is most of what you wanted to know.
If you have a date in mind

Work backwards from the date you want to swim rather than forwards from today. There are two fixed anchors. At the end, the start-up window, which is set by the finish and is not negotiable. At the front, chip-out, which cannot happen until the selections are locked and the permit set is in.

Everything between those two anchors is where a scope decision can still buy time, and the cheapest cut is an item that adds a review rather than one that adds crew days. Dropping the gas heater removes a review; dropping a color you liked removes nothing. If the scope you want does not fit the date you want, the two honest options are a smaller scope or a later date. Adding people to the job is not on the list.
On our
pool remodeling and renovation
page the scope goes in writing, with a fixed project price, before any demolition starts — which is the same deadline this article keeps coming back to. If the scope itself is still open,
what a complete remodel costs
covers the money side of the same decisions. A
project estimate
starts with a site visit, because the schedule and the price both depend on what is already in the ground.

faq.answer: The honest answer is a schedule rather than a number, because most of a remodel's calendar is not crew days. It is wait days — county reviews, inspections, material lead times and the cure on a new interior finish — plus the days spent on selections that are still open. Before demolition nobody can see what is behind the old surface, so a finish date given at signing is a best case. What a builder can tell you at that point is how many of those stops your scope contains and what starts each one.
faq.question: How long does a complete pool remodel take in Florida?

faq.answer: Very little. Almost all of the compression available happens before chip-out: locking every selection, ordering equipment at design rather than at installation, and trimming the scope items that add a review instead of the ones that add crew days. After demolition you are mostly waiting, and waiting cannot be staffed.
faq.question: Can I speed up a pool remodel once it has started?

faq.answer: From chip-out until the new interior finish is filled, and the length of that window is set by what the scope opened up rather than by the surface itself. A drained shell in Florida is a managed condition because groundwater is high in much of the state, so ask your builder how the shell is handled while it sits and what would extend that window.
faq.question: How long will my pool be empty?

faq.answer: It usually has fewer crew days and not necessarily fewer stops. Everything in a remodel is fitted to something that already exists, and what demolition exposes can add scope in the middle of the job — which is the one thing a new build does not have to absorb.
faq.question: Does a remodel take less time than building a new pool?

faq.answer: After the start-up procedure, which is set by the finish manufacturer and not by the builder. The pool is filled without stopping, the water is balanced and brushed on a schedule, and some equipment stays off until the surface has cured. Ask for that procedure in writing the day the finish goes on.

children.text: Most pool pages answer this question with a range so wide it helps nobody. The honest answer is that size, style and finish are not the whole story, and the decisions people treat as details are often the ones that move the number most.
This guide walks the eight decisions that account for most of the gap between one Florida pool and another, with what each one adds or removes. The figures come from our own
pool cost estimator
, which prices a project the same way we do.
The short answer
A custom pool of about 450 square feet with a paver deck, a pebble interior, a heater, a salt system and landscaping lands around
in Florida.
That is a starting point, not a quote. Change one decision and the number moves:
Going from the smallest pool the estimator allows to the largest is a swing of roughly
Adding a spillover spa adds about
Building the same project as a remodel instead of new construction takes roughly
off.
The rest of this guide is the eight decisions, in the order they usually get made.
1. Pool size, which moves more than anything else
Size is priced per square foot of water surface, so it compounds with every other choice you make. A larger pool needs a larger deck, more finish, more water to heat and more chemistry to balance.
From the same starting point, dropping to a 250-square-foot pool takes about
off. Going to 900 square feet adds about

This is worth deciding early for a reason that has nothing to do with money: the pool has to leave room for everything else you want in the yard. A pool sized to the maximum the setbacks allow can leave no space for the covered seating or the kitchen you also wanted.

blog.alt: Raised spa with a spillway returning to the pool, framed by a travertine deck beside a single-storey home.

children.text: 2. Pool style, which is really a construction method
Style sounds cosmetic. It is not — it changes how the shell is built.
Standard
geometry is the most efficient to form and finish.
Freeform
shapes cost more because curves take longer to form, steel and plumbing follow the curve, and the finish takes more labor.
Luxury
covers the shapes that need engineering attention: raised walls, vanishing edges, perimeter overflow.
From the same starting point, standard geometry saves about
against freeform. Luxury adds about
3. Interior finish, which decides how it ages
The interior finish is the surface you touch and the one that determines how the pool looks in year eight.
Plaster
is the baseline.
Pebble
costs more and holds its appearance longer under Florida sun and chemistry.
Premium
finishes — glass bead and the higher-end aggregates — cost the most and change the water color noticeably.
Against a pebble baseline, plaster saves about
and a premium finish adds about

Of the eight decisions, this is the one most often downgraded to protect the budget and most often regretted, because it is also the one that is expensive to change later. Replacing an interior finish means draining the pool and removing the old surface.
4. Deck material
The deck is usually larger than the pool, so its material is a bigger line than people expect.

celdas: Cheapest to install, gets hottest, shows cracks
Individually replaceable, wide range of looks
Stays coolest underfoot, most expensive to repair

children.text: From the same starting point, concrete saves about
and travertine adds about
In Florida the surface temperature question is not a detail. A deck that is uncomfortable barefoot in August is a deck that gets used less.
5. Deck size
Deck square footage is the decision most often left to the end, and it carries real money: going from a 200-square-foot deck to 1,500 is a swing of about
It is also the decision that determines whether the yard works. A pool with a deck too narrow on the long side has nowhere to put a lounger without blocking the path around the water.

blog.alt: Pool with in-water loungers and an aluminium pergola attached to the house, with newly laid turf around the deck.

children.text: 6. Spa, and which kind
There are three answers, and the middle one is where most projects land.
No spa
— nothing added.
Integrated spa
, sharing a wall with the pool, adds about
Spillover spa
, raised with water returning to the pool over a weir, adds about
A spa has to be decided before the shell is built. Adding one afterwards means cutting into a finished structure, which is why it is on this list rather than in the upgrades article.
7. What else you build at the same time
The largest single additions to a pool project are usually not the pool.
Every one of these is cheaper built alongside the pool than added later, because the crews, the access and the slab work are already on site. If an
outdoor kitchen
or a
screen enclosure
is on your list for "someday", the cheapest someday is now.
8. Site conditions, which are not optional
These are the decisions your property makes for you.
Tight access
— when equipment cannot reach the yard and material has to be moved by hand or by crane — adds about
to the whole project.
Rock excavation
adds about
HOA approval
adds a fixed amount for the drawings and submissions the association requires.
Together these can move a project by more than $18,000, and none of them are visible in a photograph of the backyard. They are the main reason an online number and a site visit disagree.

blog.alt: Two-storey Florida home with a pool, raised spa and bubblers, on a wide paver deck running the width of the yard.

children.text: What the number already includes, and what it does not

Permitting and engineering are already in the figures above, calculated against the pool and deck scope rather than as a flat fee — the drawings and reviews a project needs scale with what is being built.

What is not included: anything your county or HOA charges you directly, and anything nobody can see until the ground is open. Utility routing, an unexpected water table and a failed soil condition are all discovered, not estimated.
New build or remodel
If you already have a pool, the same finished result costs meaningfully less — roughly
less on the project above — because the excavation, the shell and much of the plumbing already exist.
That saving is real, but it is conditional. It assumes the existing shell is sound. If it is not, the comparison changes, and that is a decision worth making before you commit:
new pool construction vs pool remodeling
covers how to tell.
What to do with this
Work through the eight decisions in order and write down what you actually want before anyone quotes you. Then run the same set through the
pool cost estimator
and see which decision is moving your number most.
If the answer surprises you, that is the useful part. Most people find one decision they were treating as fixed is worth more to them than two they were arguing about.
When you have a scope you believe in, a site visit is what turns it into a price. Ours reviews access, grade and utilities before anyone quotes a number — see
custom pool and spa construction
for how the process runs.

cardTitle: What Will Your Pool Really Cost?

faq.answer: Yes. Permitting and engineering are calculated as a percentage of the pool and deck scope rather than a flat fee, because the drawings and reviews a project needs scale with what is being built. What it does not include is anything your county or HOA charges you directly, or work triggered by a condition nobody can see until excavation starts.
faq.question: Does the estimate include permits and engineering?

faq.answer: Because size is only one of eight decisions. Two 450-square-foot pools can differ by more than the price of a car once style, interior finish, deck material, deck size and spa are settled. The estimator exists to show which of those decisions is moving your number.
faq.question: Why do two pools the same size quote so differently?

faq.answer: For the same finished result, yes, because the shell, the excavation and much of the plumbing already exist. The saving is proportional rather than fixed, and it disappears if the existing shell has structural problems that only surface once the old surface comes off.
faq.question: Is a remodel cheaper than building new?

faq.answer: When the site has not been looked at. Access, grade, water table, soil and utility routing are all things that change scope and none of them can be judged from a satellite image. An estimate is a planning tool for comparing decisions; a site visit is what turns it into a price.

children.text: Our estimator prices a motorized louvered roof at
. That number comes from the same approved price table the
pool cost estimator
runs on, and it is a real figure for one ordinary structure: a powder-coated aluminum frame with motorized blades, going onto ground that is ready to take it.

What it is not is the cost of the project. A louvered roof is the only item in that table that is a roof, a machine and an electrical load at the same time, and each of those three drags in site work the line does not carry. Seven things change the scope. Six of the seven are settled before anything is ordered, which is the only reason it is worth reading about them now rather than at the quote.
What the $18,000 line actually is

A single line item, not a rate. The estimator does not ask how big the roof is, the way it asks for pool and deck square footage — it adds one figure when you tick the box. Tick it on the default configuration and the range moves from
to
The same table prices an aluminum pergola at $8,500, so the roof is about $9,500 more than the structure that looks like it from the driveway.
Which of the two you should build
is worth settling before pricing either, and
whether the motor earns its keep here
is a different question again. This page assumes you have answered both and are now trying to find out what the real number is.
Three things the line does
not
include:
The permit and the engineering.
Our estimator calculates permits and engineering as 9 percent of the pool and deck. A louvered roof is not in that base.
Getting power to it.
The drive is in the structure price. The circuit that feeds it is site work.
Anywhere for the water to go.
Closed, this is a roof. It produces runoff, and runoff has to land somewhere that genuinely drains.
Those last two are most of the distance between a structure priced at $18,000 and a project that lands well above it. Neither has anything to do with the product you chose. Both are about your yard.
1. Bays, not square feet
Most cost pages quote these by the square foot. That is not how the structure is engineered or ordered, and it is the single most useful thing to understand before you pick a size.

A louvered blade is a structural member. It spans unsupported between two beams, and every system has a maximum span its blades are rated for. Cover more than that and you do not get a longer blade — you get a
second bay
: another beam across the middle, usually posts under it, and a second run of blades.
Four consequences, all of which show up in the price:
The number steps, it does not slope.
Crossing from one bay to two costs more than the extra area suggests, because what you are buying is structure rather than surface.
A foot of size is free or expensive depending on which side of the span it falls.
Ask for the rated blade span early and size the roof against it on purpose. Shrinking a plan slightly to stay inside one bay is a real option; discovering the limit at the quote is not.
The intermediate beam lands over something.
Nobody thinks about where until it is over the middle of the dining table. Draw the furniture on the plan before the beam line is fixed.
Each bay can be its own drive, or not.

Two bays linked to one control cost less than two driven separately. Separate drives mean you can close the half over the kitchen and leave the half over the loungers open, which is either worth the money to you or is not — but decide it as a feature, not by accident.
Three numbers explain most of the gap between two quotes for the same backyard: rated blade span, number of bays, number of drives. Ask for all three in writing.
2. What it lands on, and whether it attaches

A closed louvered roof is a solid surface, so wind gets under it and tries to lift it. That uplift travels down the posts into the footings. Over the same footprint, its footings are larger than a pergola's and its anchorage is engineered rather than assumed — which is why what is already under your patio matters more here than it would for an open structure.
The common situations, and what each one costs you:
Going in with new construction.
Footings before the deck is poured. This is the cheapest moment there will ever be, and it is the same logic as every other
upgrade worth planning before construction begins
An existing paver deck.
Pavers come up, footings are dug and poured, pavers go back. Routine work; the cost is doing part of a deck twice, and it should be a line rather than a surprise.
An existing concrete slab.
Sometimes it takes the posts. Often the honest answer is cutting it and pouring a pad at each one, because a patio slab poured for foot traffic was not poured for uplift.
Attached to the house.
Trades footings for a ledger connection into a wall that can carry the load, plus the flashing detail where a roof meets a wall. It moves money rather than removing it.
Over something that is already there.
A screened porch, an old aluminum patio cover, a wood arbor. Removal and disposal are their own line, and so is repairing whatever the old structure was fastened to.
3. Where the water actually leaves
This is the most under-quoted item on a louvered roof, and the one most likely to create a new problem in a yard that did not have one.
With the blades closed, the perimeter beams are gutters and at least one post is a downspout. So the roof has a
discharge point

, and that point has to be somewhere that drains: a yard drain, a pop-up emitter, a tie into existing storm drainage. What it cannot be is the base of the house, the low corner of the patio, or the property line.

blog.alt: White louvered roof on square posts seen from below against a clear sky, over paving still wet after rain, with a square drain grate set into the floor and palms with dry brown fronds beyond the far edge of the roof.

children.text: What moves this line:
How far the discharge is from anything that actually drains.
Whether the run crosses finished paving, a deck, or a lawn with irrigation already in it.
Whether the lot falls toward the house, which is common enough here to be worth checking rather than assuming.
Whether the post that carries the water happens to land where water is already collecting.
Ask for it as its own line and ask
where it terminates
. "It drains through the post" answers a different question — it describes the inside of the structure, not the outside of it. What the roof does in a real storm, and what it does in wind, is
covered separately
; here it is purely a budget item.
4. The circuit, not the motor
The drive is in the structure price. The electricity to it is not, and it is the line that varies most from one house to the next.

blog.alt: Louvered roof with a dark bronze frame and cream blades seen from below, attached to a modern white house with floor-to-ceiling black-framed glass, a palm frond shadow falling across the blades and a black safety fence behind the posts.

children.text: What changes it:
Distance from the panel.
A roof off the back of the house near the service is one number. A roof on the far side of the yard is trenching and conduit.
Whether the panel has room.
If it does not, a panel upgrade is its own project with its own permit, and it is better found now than at rough-in.
What the run has to cross.
Conduit under a lawn is cheap. Conduit under finished travertine is not.
Whether there is already a subpanel out there.
A pool equipment pad changes this conversation completely, which is one more reason the roof is cheaper as part of a pool project than after it.
Controls sit here too — wall switch, remote, rain sensor, or joining whatever already runs the house. Small money against a project of this size, and cheap to decide now.
5. How much the roof is expected to carry
Lights, fans, heaters, speakers, motorized side screens. None of it is in the $18,000, and all of it is cheaper to
allow for
than to add.

The frame is hollow, so the sleeves and conduit for those runs go in while the structure is open. You do not have to buy the fixtures up front; you have to leave them somewhere to go. Wiring planned before assembly disappears inside the beams. Wiring added afterwards runs on the surface, and that is visible for as long as the structure stands.

blog.alt: White louvered roof over an outdoor dining area next to the covered porch of a two-story house, with a ceiling fan under the adjoining porch, two mismatched dining sets below and palms over a white picket fence.

children.text: One item genuinely cannot be retrofitted cleanly:
side screens
. Their channels mount to the posts, so adding them later means opening finished work. Decide where they go even if you buy them in two years — the same rule that applies to
the features worth planning alongside a poolside pergola
. How the lights, fans and screens work together as one system is
its own subject
, and it is worth reading before you finalize the frame rather than after.
6. Engineering, the permit, and which county you are in

A closed louvered roof is reviewed as a roof. That means its wind uplift, its anchorage and its drainage are all part of the submission, and the drawings are sealed for the design wind speed at your specific address — not for Florida generally. An inland North Florida lot and a coastal South Florida one do not get the same structure from the same catalog.
Two practical effects on your number:
Engineering is a real line.
A price with no engineering in it is a price for a structure nobody has checked. Ask whether sealed drawings are included or extra.
The review is a county process

, and the sequence differs between them. Have the contractor pull the permit under their own license — a contractor asking you to pull an owner-builder permit is transferring liability for the structure to you. The shape of that process is described in
whether you need a permit for a pergola in Florida
, and it applies here with the roof review added on top.
7. The two site conditions the estimator does price
Both are checkboxes rather than judgement calls, and both apply to the whole project, the roof line included.
Difficult access: 8 percent.
The same $18,000 roof is
on a lot where the machine cannot get around the house. On the default configuration, the range goes from $99,000 – $122,000 to
. A narrow side gate, a slope, a septic field that cannot be crossed, a tree that stays.
HOA review: $1,500.
A flat line in the estimator. The fee is the easy part; the calendar is the cost, because the board meets when it meets and the review happens
before
the permit application rather than alongside it.
Which decisions stay open, and which close

celdas: Which way it moves the price
Can it change after the build?
Steps up at the span limit, not gradually
No — it sets the whole frame
Sideways: footings against a wall connection
Small if planned, large if solved later

children.text: Reading two louvered roof quotes
If both totals are close, they are almost certainly describing different projects. The scope lines to compare, in the order they cause arguments:
Rated blade span, number of bays, number of drives.
Engineering and sealed drawings: included, or extra.
Who pulls the permit and meets the inspector.
Where the water terminates, and who digs to get it there.
What electrical is included, who performs it, and whether a panel upgrade is assumed away.
What is roughed in now and what is capped for later.
What happens to the existing deck or slab, and who puts it back.
The warranty, split out: structure, finish, motor and controls, labor. Those are four different terms and "fully warrantied" covers none of them.
That is the scope conversation. The product conversation — blade profile, drive type, how the seals are made — is
a comparison of its own
, and what to ask the company rather than about the roof is in
questions to ask before hiring an installer
What to do with the number
Run the
pool cost estimator
twice — once with the louvered roof ticked, once without — and look at what it does to the total rather than at the line by itself. What comes back is a
plus or minus 10 percent

range built from the same approved price table as every figure on this page. It is built to show you which of your decisions is moving your number, not to quote your project. If the timing is the constraint rather than the scope,
financing
changes when rather than what, and the decisions above do not get cheaper by waiting.
For a real figure, the span, the anchorage, the discharge point and the panel all have to be looked at on the ground. How we build these is on the
motorized louvered roof systems
page,
the gallery
has finished ones in real backyards, and a
project evaluation
starts with that walk-through rather than with a number over the phone.

faq.answer: Our estimator prices a motorized louvered roof at $18,000 as one line on a backyard project. That figure is the structure: one ordinary frame with motorized blades, landing on ground that is ready to take it. What the estimator returns overall is a range of plus or minus 10 percent, not a quote.
faq.question: How much does a motorized louvered roof cost?

faq.answer: Because the blade is a structural member with a rated unsupported span. Past that span you do not get a longer blade, you get a second bay with its own beam, posts and run of blades. The price steps at that line rather than sloping with area, which is why two roofs of similar size can be quoted very differently.
faq.question: Why is a louvered roof not priced by the square foot?

faq.answer: No. Our estimator calculates permits and engineering as 9 percent of the pool and deck, and a louvered roof is not part of that base. Built on its own it is permitted, engineered and inspected as its own project, and that cost sits outside the line.
faq.question: Is the permit included in the estimator's $18,000 line?

faq.answer: The drive needs power on a dedicated circuit, and that is site work rather than part of the structure price. What it costs depends on how far the panel is, whether the panel has capacity left, and whether the run has to cross paving that is already finished.
faq.question: Does a motorized louvered roof need its own electrical circuit?

faq.answer: Lights and fans can, if conduit was sleeved through the frame while it was open. Side screens are the one item that does not retrofit cleanly, because the channels mount to the posts and adding them afterwards means opening finished work. Decide where they go even if you buy them later.

children.text: A complete pool remodel in Florida — new interior finish, new waterline tile and coping, a rebuilt equipment pad and a replaced deck — runs about

on our estimator's default project: a 450-square-foot freeform pool with a pebble interior, a 600-square-foot paver deck, a heater, salt chlorination, three lights and landscaping. That figure comes from our own
pool cost estimator
, which prices a remodel at 82% of what the same finished result would cost as new construction and publishes every total as a ±10% band.
The second half of that sentence is the part worth understanding.
A remodel is not priced from what is wrong with your pool. It is priced from the finished result you are buying, minus the work you already paid for once.
The hole, the shell and most of the plumbing are already there. Everything else is quoted the same way it would be on a new build.
That has a consequence most homeowners do not expect: the age and condition of your pool barely appear in the arithmetic. Condition decides
whether
a remodel makes sense. Scope decides what it costs.
The numbers, and where they come from
The same estimator, run on the same project both ways:

celdas: 250 sq ft pool, 200 sq ft deck (the smallest the sliders go)
450 sq ft pool, 600 sq ft deck
900 sq ft pool, 600 sq ft deck

children.text: All three are the same specification — freeform shape, pebble interior, paver deck, permitting and engineering, a heater, a salt system, three LED lights and landscaping — with only the two sizes changed. The range we publish is the middle figure ±10%. Unless a number below is called out as a line in the breakdown, every remodel-path figure in this guide is what the estimator's total moves by when you change one input and leave the rest alone.
Two things fall out of this table.
The saving is a percentage, not a coupon.

It grows with the project. On the smallest project the estimator models it is worth about $10,000; on the largest, nearly $28,000. Anyone quoting you a flat "remodels save about $15,000" is quoting the middle of a curve.
Everything you choose during a remodel is also discounted.
A spillover spa that adds $18,000 to a new build adds about
on the remodel path. A screen enclosure that lists at $15,000 adds about
. The crews, the access and the site setup are being paid for once either way.
The 18% saving is conditional
That 18% — the gap between the remodel price and the new-build price — assumes the shell is sound. It is the entire load-bearing assumption in the number, and the one thing an estimator cannot check.

If the structure has moved, if the steel has corroded through, or if the shape itself is the problem, the credit you are being given for "the shell already exists" shrinks toward nothing — and at some point rebuilding is the cheaper honest answer. That comparison is a diagnosis rather than a budget exercise, and
remodel or rebuild
is where to make it before you start pricing scope. If you are still deciding between renovating what you have and starting over on a new pool entirely,
new pool construction vs pool remodeling
covers that fork.
Assume for the rest of this guide that the shell is fine. Four things then decide what the remodel costs.
1. How far down the demolition goes
This is the biggest fork in the road, and it is not really about the pool. It is about the edge.

celdas: The first band of deck, necessarily

children.text: Where the line falls between the first row and the other two is the subject of
resurfacing versus a full renovation
; what follows here is what each one does to the number.

Waterline tile and coping sit exactly where the deck meets the water. Removing them means cutting into the deck edge, and a repaired band of twenty-year-old concrete next to new coping rarely looks like anything other than a repaired band. That is why the middle option tends to slide into the third one on site: once you have opened the edge, replacing the deck is the difference between a remodel that looks new and one that looks patched.
The deck is also where the money is. On the remodel path, running the deck slider from 200 square feet to 1,500 is a swing of about
, and choosing travertine over concrete on a 600-square-foot deck is another
. The deck is usually larger than the pool, so it behaves like the larger line item it is. (The material trade-offs — heat underfoot, repairability — are covered in
what a custom pool really costs
; they are identical on a remodel.)
Inside the water, the interior finish carries the other swing: plaster to a premium aggregate is about

on this project. It is the decision most often trimmed to protect a budget, and the one that is most expensive to revisit, because changing it later means draining the pool and removing a surface you just paid for.

blog.alt: Pool and spa edged in travertine, with in-water loungers at the shallow end, patio furniture under the lanai and the neighbor's metal fence behind.

children.text: 2. Whether the shell keeps its shape

A remodel that resurfaces the existing shape is one kind of project. A remodel that changes the shape — squaring off a kidney, raising a wall, adding a sun shelf or a vanishing edge — is new construction performed inside an existing hole.

Our estimator carries three shape tiers — standard, freeform and luxury — at $85, $110 and $145 per square foot before the finish multiplier. On the remodel path, a 450-square-foot pool moving from the standard tier to the luxury one is about
; from the freeform default to luxury, about
. That gap is real work: new steel, new forming, new plumbing runs, and a structural tie between old shell and new.

It is also the point where the 18% credit starts to erode, because you are demolishing the part of the pool you were being credited for. If more than a wall or two is changing, price it both ways before committing.
3. What the equipment pad has to become

A pool built twenty years ago was plumbed for the pad of its day: a single-speed pump, no automation, and lights that were not LEDs. The pad is usually the cheapest meaningful upgrade in the project, and the easiest one to leave out of a budget.
On the remodel path our estimator adds roughly:
for a heater
for automation
for a salt system
$370 per LED light

The reason to decide this now rather than later is procedural, not financial. Touching the equipment pad generally pulls electrical work — and the bonding of everything metallic around the pool — into the same permit and the same inspection as the rest of the remodel. Done during the project, it is one review. Done in two years, it is its own permit, its own inspection, and a second trip for a crew.
What permits are required for pool construction in Florida
covers how the reviews stack, and it works the same way on a renovation.
4. What your yard has become since the pool was built
This is the factor that separates remodel pricing from new-build pricing, and it is the one that rarely appears in a budget.

The builder who dug your pool had an open lot. Today that same yard may have a screen enclosure over it, a side gate too narrow for a mini excavator, an A/C pad, a paver walkway, an irrigation system and twenty years of root growth. Every cubic yard of demolition debris has to leave through that, and every pallet of coping has to come in the same way.
Our estimator prices restricted access at
8% of the entire project
— about
on the 450-square-foot remodel above. Rock excavation, where it applies, is
, roughly
. Together they move this project by more than
, and neither is visible in a photo of the backyard.
On new construction, tight access is the exception. On remodels it is closer to the default, and it is a common reason an online number and a site visit disagree.

blog.alt: Aerial view of a rectangular pool with a raised square spa and a travertine deck, two poolside basketball hoops, a coiled green hose on the house wall and a neighbor's screened pool enclosure beyond the hedge.

children.text: What no estimate knows until the surface comes off
Four things are discovered rather than estimated:
Hollow spots
behind the old finish, where the surface has delaminated from the shell.
Corroded steel
, usually where a crack has been letting water reach it for years.
Plumbing buried in the shell wall
that has to be rerouted rather than reused.
A deck bonded to the coping
more thoroughly than anyone expected, which turns a partial deck repair into a full replacement.

None of these are unusual. What matters is how the contract handles them: whether there is an allowance, who approves the extra work, and whether you see a priced change order before it happens rather than on the final invoice. That question, and the others worth asking before signing anything, are in
how to choose a pool builder in Florida
A remodel quote with no language about what happens below the surface is not a lower quote. It is an incomplete one.
The things that are cheapest while the pool is open
Anything that needs the deck opened, the pad rebuilt or a crew in the backyard is cheaper now than it will ever be again. On the remodel path our estimator prices these additions at:
The same structures added two years after the remodel cost their full new-build price, plus the cost of cutting into a deck you just paid to install. If a
screen enclosure
or an
outdoor kitchen
is on a someday list, the remodel is the someday.
Which upgrades genuinely have to happen now and which are fine to defer is a separate sorting exercise, and
what to upgrade during a complete pool remodel
works through it item by item.

blog.alt: Aerial view of a pool and spa beside a covered outdoor kitchen under a metal roof, with a daybed on the porch and worn patches in the surrounding lawn.

children.text: Permits and engineering scale with what you touch

Permitting and engineering are already inside every figure above. Our estimator charges them at 9% of the pool plus the deck rather than as a flat fee, so it moves with the scope: on the 450-square-foot project the estimator's Permits & Engineering line reads about
, and it reaches the remodel total at the same 82% as everything else. A project that leaves the deck alone carries a visibly smaller permitting line than one that replaces it.

What sits outside those figures: whatever your county or HOA charges you directly. The review process is set by the county, not by the state, so the sequence and the fees in Alachua are not the sequence and the fees in Broward. What is constant is that the work should be permitted and inspected under the license of the company you contracted with, and that you can verify that license yourself in the state's public register.
What to do with this

Decide the finished result first — deck size, deck material, interior finish, whether the shape changes, what the equipment pad becomes — and price that. Do not start from what is broken; that tells you why you are remodeling, not what it costs.
Then run the same set of decisions through the
pool cost estimator
with the project type set to remodel, and watch which one moves your number most. For most people it is the deck, and most people expect it to be the finish.
When you have a scope you believe in, a site visit is what turns it into a price. Access, the condition of the shell and what the deck is actually bonded to all need to be looked at — see
complete pool remodeling and renovation
for how we run one, or
request an estimate
to start with the walkthrough rather than a number.

faq.answer: Because the excavation, the shell and most of the plumbing already exist and are not being paid for a second time. Our estimator prices a remodel at 82% of the same finished result built new, so the saving is a proportion of the scope rather than a fixed amount. On a larger project it is worth more; on a small one, less.
faq.question: Why is a pool remodel cheaper than building new?

faq.answer: Far less than most people expect. Condition decides whether a remodel is the right move at all, and scope decides what it costs. A twenty-year-old pool and a ten-year-old pool finished to the same specification price almost identically, as long as both shells are sound.
faq.question: Does the price depend on how old or how bad my pool is?

faq.answer: Sometimes, and it is the cheapest version of the job. The constraint is the edge: waterline tile and coping sit where the deck meets the pool, so replacing them usually means cutting and repairing the first band of deck. If the coping stays, the deck can stay too.
faq.question: Can I resurface without touching the deck?

faq.answer: Because the shell is only visible once the old surface comes off. Hollow spots, corroded steel and plumbing buried in the shell wall are discovered rather than estimated. Ask before signing how the contract handles what is found, and what the approval step is before that work proceeds.
faq.question: Why would a remodel quote change after work starts?

children.text: Our estimator carries a new pool screen enclosure as a single $15,000 line, and it shows every total in a band of plus or minus 10 percent. That figure describes a cage designed alongside a new pool and deck, on a site with ordinary access, where the concrete underneath it was poured knowing the cage was coming.

Three things move it from there, and only one of them is the size of your backyard. The cage's height and clear span decide how much aluminum is in it. The wind load your structure is engineered to decides how thick that aluminum has to be and how often it is anchored. And the concrete under the posts decides whether the footings are already in the ground or have to be cut into a finished deck.
That third one is the expensive one, it is invisible in every photograph, and it is the only item on the list that stops being cheap on a specific day: the day the deck sets.
Three prices arriving as one

celdas: Posts, beams, chair rails, fasteners, bracing
Height, clear span, and the load the engineer designs to
Footings, anchors, and the connection to the house
Whether the concrete was poured for a cage, or is being drilled after the fact
Mesh choice, panel width, and how many doors

children.text: Homeowners shop the third line, argue about the first, and rarely ask about the second. The second is where two quotes for "the same cage" actually separate, because it is the only one that never appears in a rendering.
Price follows surface and span, not deck footprint
The screen on a pool enclosure is the roof plus the walls. Your deck footprint sets the roof.
Height sets the walls, on all four sides at once.

Raise a cage two feet over the same deck and you have not added two feet. You have added a band of screen around the entire perimeter, longer posts, and — because those posts are now carrying more load over more distance — a heavier post and beam schedule underneath the whole thing. Height is the single most common reason two enclosures over identical decks are priced well apart.

Clear span does the same work sideways. Every upright you take out of a sightline has to be paid for in a deeper beam. That is the honest trade behind wide-panel and panoramic framing: the view is real, and so is the aluminum it takes to hold the opening. Which one suits the yard is a look-and-feel question. What it costs is an engineering one, and it is settled by where the uprights land — so ask for the post layout on the drawing, not a description of the view.

Roof profile is the third dimension of the same question. A flatter profile carries a shorter span and looks lower from the yard; a steeper one sheds rain and debris more readily and adds height at the ridge, along with everything height brings with it. These are not interchangeable styling options with one price.

blog.alt: Pool and raised spa inside a screen enclosure, with a stone water feature spilling into the pool at one end, lounge chairs and a fire table on the travertine deck, and a lake beyond the mesh.

children.text: The wind load is a property-level number, not a Florida number

A pool enclosure is an engineered structure. Somebody seals drawings for your address, a plan reviewer in your county checks them, and an inspector verifies that what went up matches what was sealed. That sequence is not a formality — it is most of what you are buying when you buy a cage rather than a carport.
Two inputs into those drawings change the aluminum, and both are specific to your lot rather than to the state:
The design wind speed at your address.
It is not uniform across Florida, and it is not uniform across a county either.
The exposure the site actually has.

A lot backing onto open water or a wide lake is not in the same situation as an identical lot screened by two-story houses on three sides. The engineer takes a position on that, and the position shows up as extrusion sizes, anchor spacing and cable bracing.
This gives you the most useful question in the entire comparison, and almost nobody asks it:
what design wind speed and what exposure category was this quote engineered to?
Two bidders who answered that differently have not given you two prices. They have given you two structures. Ask for both figures in writing, on the quote itself.

Be equally direct about what happens afterwards. A cage is a permitted, inspected structure, and it should be permitted under the license of the contractor building it — which you can confirm yourself in the state's public register before signing anything.
What permits are required for pool construction in Florida
covers how the reviews stack up when the pool and the enclosure are happening together.
The footings are the line nobody plans for

The posts do not stand on the deck. They stand on concrete that has to be thick enough and reinforced enough to hold a structure down in wind, and a pool deck poured without a cage in mind is not automatically that concrete.
Which side of this you land on is decided by timing, not by budget.
If the pool and deck are being built now,

the cage is drawn first and the deck is poured to receive it: thickened edges and footings go in while the ground is open and the forms are already set. The incremental cost of doing it in that order is close to nothing, and it is the reason our estimator's $15,000 line is a realistic planning number in a new build.
If the deck is already finished,

the work becomes demolition. Cores get drilled; where the slab turns out to be too thin or unreinforced, sections are cut out, new footings are poured, and the surface is put back. Our estimator prices decking at $12 a square foot for concrete, $22 for pavers and $35 for travertine, which gives you a sense of what is being cut into — and the patch never quite matches the field around it, no matter which of the three it is. Pavers are the forgiving case, because they can be lifted and reset. Poured concrete and travertine are not forgiving.
So the decision that saves the most money here costs almost nothing to make and has to be made early:
if an enclosure is even a possibility, have the deck designed for one.
That belongs on the same list as the other things worth settling while the design is still on paper, in
upgrades worth planning before construction begins
, and next to the questions to answer before any of it starts, in
what to decide before you build a pool in Florida

blog.alt: Curved pool and raised spa under a white-framed screen enclosure, with white Adirondack chairs around a round table on a painted concrete deck and an exterior staircase climbing to the teal-sided upper floor of the house.

children.text: Where it meets the house
Most cages attach to the house along one side, and that joint is where enclosure projects generate their long-term complaints.

The beam at the house normally doubles as a gutter, which means the roof edge above it has to drain into it and the fascia below it has to carry structural load. Whether that detail is straightforward depends on what your roof is made of and what condition the fascia is in, and both are things a bidder should have looked at rather than assumed. Ask directly what happens at the house: where the water goes, what the existing gutter does once the cage is up, and who is responsible if the fascia turns out to be soft.

One related habit worth naming, because it shows up on finished cages constantly: the frame is an engineered structure, not a hanging rail. Fans, lights, televisions, shade cloth and sports hardware all end up bolted to cages, and each of them is load the sealed drawings never saw. If you want any of it, say so before the drawings are sealed. Afterwards it is a modification to an engineered structure.

blog.alt: Screen enclosure meeting the house at a covered lanai with a ceiling fan and a built-in grill island, the paver deck running down to a freeform pool, with a lake and power lines beyond the cage.

children.text: Screen, doors, and the question the county answers

Mesh is normally presented last, as a comfort preference. It is worth moving earlier for one reason that rarely gets explained: tighter weaves stop more insects and more light, and they also pass less air, which means the frame catches more wind. That makes the mesh an engineering input, not a finish. Choose it before the drawings are sealed, and ask what each weave costs you in airflow and view before picking the tightest one on the shelf.

Doors are a count, and the count matters more than the door. Each one is an opening in the structure, hardware, and a place the mesh gets handled every day. Two doors on a cage that needs one is a small permanent expense in a place that takes wear.

Then there is the question that is not yours to answer: whether the enclosure is being counted as the pool's safety barrier. Where it is, the door hardware becomes part of the plan review rather than a preference, and that is settled by the reviewer in your county rather than by the catalogue. Ask your builder which way it is being submitted, and get the answer before the doors are ordered.

If there is an existing cage coming down first, its removal and disposal is a separate line and should appear as one. Whether it needs to come down at all is worth asking before it is assumed: a frame that is still sound and a screen that is finished are two different jobs at two different prices.
Eight lines that make two quotes comparable
Enclosure bids are famously hard to read side by side because most of them describe the result rather than the structure. These make them comparable:
Height at the house and at the far end, and the roof profile.
The design wind speed and exposure category the engineering assumes.
Post and beam sizes, and exactly where the uprights land.
What is assumed about the existing concrete, and what happens if it proves too thin — priced, or a change order.
The connection at the house: gutter detail, fascia condition, and who owns the roof edge.
Mesh type, panel by panel, and whether it was priced before or after the engineering.
Door count, hardware, and whether the enclosure is being submitted as the barrier.
Removal and disposal of the existing cage, if there is one.
None of these are traps. A builder who runs these projects will answer all eight quickly, and the speed of the answers tells you nearly as much as their content — which is most of
how to tell one pool builder from another
The order that keeps this from going wrong
Three decisions, in this sequence:
Whether you want one at all.

A cage changes how the yard looks and how it is used, in both directions, and that trade-off is worth settling before anyone measures. It is also where a screen enclosure gets compared with the alternatives that are not really alternatives: our estimator prices an aluminum pergola at $8,500 and a motorized louvered roof at $18,000, and none of the three does the other's job — the two alternatives are priced out in
what an aluminum pergola costs in Florida
and
what a motorized louvered roof costs
How high and how open.
Height, panel width and roof profile, decided together, because each one moves the other two and all three move the price.
What it stands on.
The deck detail and the footings — which has a deadline, and the deadline is the pour.

Taking those out of order is what produces the two expensive surprises on this kind of project: a finished deck cut open for footings, and a cage redesigned after the drawings were sealed. The order is free. The corrections are not.
If you want to see how we scope one — site walk, exposure, height and span, then the deck detail — that is on the
pool screen enclosures
page, and finished cages from our own jobs are in the
project gallery
. To see the $15,000 line sitting inside a whole backyard budget rather than on its own, the
pool cost estimator
puts it next to the pool, the deck and everything else — and if you are still working out the pool itself,
what a custom pool really costs
is the companion to this one. A
project estimate
starts with the site visit, which for an enclosure mostly means looking at what is behind your lot and what is under your deck.

faq.answer: Our estimator carries a screen enclosure as a single $15,000 line and shows every total in a band of plus or minus 10 percent. That is a planning figure for a cage designed alongside a new pool and deck, on a site with ordinary access. Height, clear span, the engineered wind load and the condition of the concrete under the posts all move it from there.
faq.question: How much does a pool screen enclosure cost in Florida?

faq.answer: Less than people expect. Footprint sets the roof area, but the walls are set by height, and height also drives post and beam sizes. A taller cage over the same deck is a bigger structure in every direction, which is why two enclosures covering identical decks can be quoted well apart.
faq.question: Does a bigger pool deck mean a more expensive cage?

faq.answer: Usually the engineering assumptions rather than the aluminum. Ask each bidder what design wind speed and what exposure category the drawings were engineered to, and where the uprights land. Two quotes engineered to different assumptions are two different structures, not two prices for one.
faq.question: Why are two pool enclosure quotes so far apart?

faq.answer: Yes, but the footings are the variable. The posts need concrete beneath them with adequate thickness and reinforcement, and an existing deck may or may not have it. Where it does not, sections get cut out, new footings are poured and the surface is patched, and the patch rarely matches the field around it.
faq.question: Can a screen enclosure be added to a pool deck that is already finished?

faq.answer: It can. Tighter weaves block more insects and more light, and they also let less air pass, which means the frame catches more wind. Mesh is usually presented as a comfort choice, but it is an input the engineer needs before the drawings are sealed rather than a finish selected at the end.
faq.question: Does the screen mesh I choose affect the structure?

children.text: Our estimator prices an aluminum pergola at
. That number comes from the same approved price table the
pool cost estimator
runs on, and it is a real figure for an ordinary structure: one pergola, ordinary post spacing, landing on ground that is ready to take it.

What it is not is a price per pergola. Six decisions move that line, and only one of them is size. The rest are structural, they are all made before anything is ordered, and they are the reason two pergola quotes can carry the same total and describe different buildings.
What the $8,500 line actually is

It is a single line item, not a rate. The estimator does not ask how big the pergola is, the way it asks for pool and deck square footage — it adds one figure when you tick the box. That is a deliberate simplification and it holds for the ordinary case.
Tick it on the estimator's default configuration and the range moves from
to
. Which is the honest way to see a pergola in a backyard project: not as a separate purchase, but as roughly a tenth added to the yard.
Two things that line does
not
include:
The permit.
Our estimator calculates permits and engineering as 9 percent of the pool and deck. The pergola is not in that base.
Anything the pergola is meant to hold.
Fans, lights, screens, a heater, speakers. Those are separate, and what they cost later depends on what was run through the posts before they were closed.
1. Span, not square feet
This is the factor that moves the price most and the one homeowners almost never ask about.

People size a pergola by area. Aluminum is priced by what a beam has to carry across an unsupported distance. Take the same footprint and remove two posts to open one side, and you have not saved two footings — you have doubled the clear span, and the beam depth and the wall thickness of the extrusion both have to go up to carry it.

A structure with a post at every corner and one with a long open side can be identical on a floor plan and different on an order sheet. If you want an open side — because it faces the water, or because a post would land where the table goes — that belongs in the first design conversation, not in a change order after the members are ordered.
2. What it lands on
The pergola is only as cheap as the ground under it. In rough order, from least to most expensive:
A pool project still under construction.
Footings go in before the deck is poured. This is the cheapest moment there will ever be, and it is covered in
the upgrades worth planning before construction starts
An existing concrete slab.
Workable, if it is thick enough and reinforced where the posts land. Sometimes it is, and sometimes the honest answer is a poured pad at each post.
An existing paver deck.
Pavers come up, footings get dug and poured, pavers go back. The work is routine; the cost is the labor of doing a deck twice.
Attached to the house.
Trades footings for a ledger connection, a flashing detail and a wall that can take the load. Whether attached or freestanding is the right layout is
a decision of its own
; as a price factor, it moves money from the ground to the wall rather than removing it.
What the footing work involves in each case, and the point at which it stops being free, is the sequencing question in
the seven pergola decisions that close before construction
. For reading a quote, only one thing has to be settled: which of the four rows above you are in. A contractor who has not asked is pricing a different one.

blog.alt: Gabled aluminum patio cover attached to a stucco house, with a weathered wall lantern beside it and a white PVC fence behind.

children.text: 3. Wind load, which is set by the lot

Every permanent structure in Florida is engineered for a design wind speed, and that speed is set by where the lot sits — not by the state as a whole. A coastal South Florida site carries a stricter requirement than an inland North Florida one, and the practical effect is that the same drawing does not carry from one county to the next. Heavier members, more anchors, deeper footings.
For the quote, this has one clear consequence:
engineering is a real line, and sealed drawings are what the building department reviews.
A price with no engineering in it is a price for a structure nobody has checked. What the permit process itself looks like, county by county, is in
whether you need a permit for a pergola in Florida
4. Fixed slats or operable louvers
This is the largest single fork available, and the estimator prices both sides of it:
for a pergola,
for a motorized louvered roof. The gap is $9,500 — more than the pergola costs.
That money buys moving parts, a motor, controls and a rain path that closes, which changes the structure rather than just the top of it. It is a different build, not an upgrade tier, and
which one you should build

is worth settling before you price either. The mistake to avoid is pricing a pergola, deciding later that you wanted the roof to close, and discovering that the posts and footings were sized for the lighter structure.
5. What runs through the posts

Aluminum posts are hollow, and the wire for lights, fans, retractable screens, a heater or speakers runs inside them and through the footings. Done while the frame is still open, it is a small line: conduit and an electrician's hours.

It is small only once. The same fixtures added afterwards mean surface conduit down a finished post, or a trench across a deck that is already laid — and that second bill lands against the deck, not against the pergola, which is why it never appears in the comparison people think they are making. You do not have to buy the fixtures up front. You do have to leave them somewhere to go.
Which provisions are worth leaving, and why it is settled at fabrication rather than at purchase, is
decision six of the seven that close before construction
. Screens, lights and fans follow the same logic on the sides and overhead:
they are designed into the frame, not added to it

blog.alt: Modern aluminum pergola beside a pool with two black electrical cables left hanging from the frame, waiting for light fixtures.

children.text: 6. Site conditions the estimator does price

Three of them, and all three are checkboxes rather than judgement calls. Two are percentage surcharges on the whole project, which means they move the pergola line even when the condition has nothing to do with the pergola:
Difficult access: 8 percent.

A gate too narrow, a slope, a septic field that cannot be crossed, a tree that stays. Our estimator applies it to the whole project, the pergola line included, so the same pergola that is $8,500 on an open lot is
on that one.
Rock excavation: 12 percent.
The rock is under the pool, not under the pergola — but our estimator surcharges the project total the same way, so the pergola line reads
with it ticked, and
with both. Worth knowing before you read the pergola line on a pool quote as a pergola price.
HOA review: $1,500.
A flat line, and the fee is the easy part. The calendar cost is a board that meets when it meets, and the review normally has to clear before the permit application rather than alongside it.

blog.alt: Aluminum pergola on a waterfront lot beside a canal, with freshly staked palms to the left and loose garden spotlights sitting on gravel.

children.text: Which decisions are still open later

celdas: Which way it moves the price
Can it change after the build?

Sideways: footings against a wall connection
A small line now, a large one later

children.text: How to tell two pergola quotes apart
Two totals within a few hundred dollars of each other usually mean two different buildings. Ask both:
How many posts, and what is the longest clear span?
The answer explains most of the price difference on its own.
What is the wall thickness of the extrusion?
"Aluminum" is not a specification. Two structures of identical dimensions can be built from very different members.
Are engineering and sealed drawings included, or extra?
Who pulls the permit and meets the inspector?
It should be the contractor, under their own license. A contractor asking you to pull an owner-builder permit is transferring the liability for the structure to you.
How does it anchor, and what happens to the existing deck?
Lifting and resetting pavers is normal work; it should also be a line rather than a surprise.
What is roughed in for power, and what is capped for later?
What is the finish warranty, and on what exactly?
The structure, the powder coat and the hardware are usually three separate things. Why aluminum holds up the way it does in this climate — and what it holds up better than — is covered in
aluminum against wood over a Florida decade
When $8,500 is not the question you are asking

If the pergola is going beside a pool, over a kitchen, or in front of a screen room, it is not really a standalone purchase — it is one structure in a backyard that has to be laid out at once, because the footings, the conduit, the drainage and the deck all cross each other underground.
Planning a pergola beside a pool
and
the outdoor living design guide
both start from the whole yard rather than from one structure, which is the order the ground actually requires.
What to do with all of this
Run the
pool cost estimator
twice — once with the pergola ticked, once without — and look at what it does to the total rather than at the line on its own. What comes out is a
plus or minus 10 percent
range built from the same approved price table as every figure above. It is meant to tell you which of your decisions is moving your number, not to quote your project.
Then, for a real figure, the span, the anchoring and the wind design all have to be looked at on site. How that works is on the
custom aluminum pergola page
, and a
project evaluation
starts with the site visit rather than with a number over the phone.

faq.answer: Our estimator prices an aluminum pergola at $8,500 as a single line on a project. That figure assumes an ordinary structure with ordinary post spacing, going onto ground that is ready to take it. What the estimator returns overall is a range of plus or minus 10 percent, not a quote.
faq.question: How much does an aluminum pergola cost in Florida?

faq.answer: Area matters less than the longest unsupported span. Two structures with the same footprint can be priced differently because one has a post at every corner and the other leaves a side open, which forces deeper beams and heavier extrusions. Ask for the span and the post count before comparing sizes.
faq.question: Does a bigger pergola always cost more?

faq.answer: No. Our estimator calculates permits and engineering as 9 percent of the pool and deck, and the pergola is not part of that base. A pergola built on its own is permitted, engineered and inspected as its own project, and that cost sits outside the $8,500.
faq.question: Is the permit included in the estimator's pergola line?

faq.answer: Our estimator prices a motorized louvered roof at $18,000 against $8,500 for a pergola. The difference buys moving parts, a motor, controls and a sealed rain path, which changes the structure rather than just the top of it. Whether that gap is worth it depends on what you want the space to do in the rain.
faq.question: Why is a louvered roof more than twice the price of a pergola?

faq.answer: They can, but the cost depends entirely on whether conduit was run inside the posts and footings while the structure was open. Added afterwards, the wiring is either surface-mounted or trenched, and neither is as clean or as cheap as a sleeve placed before the concrete went in.
faq.question: Can lighting and fans be added to a pergola later?
