children.text: A pergola beside a pool is not a pergola that happens to be near water. Most of the decisions below change
because
there is water there, and four of them stop being cheap the day the deck is poured.

That is the entire argument for planning the two together. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 whether it goes up with the pool or five years after it. The pergola is not where the money moves. The deck is.
If you take two things from this: decide where the posts land before the deck is poured, and choose the deck material knowing whether a pergola is coming.
The window you are actually working in
Most people arrive at this decision in one of three states, and the state decides how much of the list is still open.

celdas: Post positions, footings, conduit, drainage, bonding
Post positions — pavers lift and reset
Deck poured in concrete or mortar-set stone
Post positions, unless you saw-cut and patch

children.text: None of those is a bad place to be. The third one just costs more to change your mind in, and most people do not know they have walked into it until the pergola contractor is standing on the deck with a tape.
Four decisions that close when the deck does
1. Where the posts land
A pergola post is not held down by its own weight. In Florida it is engineered against uplift, which means a footing sized for the structure — not an anchor bolt into a thin deck slab.

Beside a pool, that footing has to miss three buried things: the pool's bond beam and shell, the plumbing runs between the skimmer, the returns and the equipment pad, and the conduit feeding the light niche. Where those run is known precisely on exactly one day — the day they go in. After that it is memory, a drawing if someone kept one, and a locator.
That is the practical case for one plan instead of two. The information you need to place a footing safely exists at the start and decays afterwards.

There is a comfort dimension too. Measure the walkway from the water's edge, not from the house wall. A post set tight to the coping turns the busiest side of the deck into a corridor, and nobody notices on a drawing.

blog.alt: Dark-framed pergola on a pool deck, with overhead utility lines crossing the sky and a faded wooden gate in the back fence.

children.text: 2. Which side of the pool, and how far back
The Florida problem is the four o'clock sun, not the noon sun.

At noon, shade lands under the structure, which is where everyone assumes it always lands. By late afternoon the sun is low in the west and that shade has moved well to the east of the posts. A pergola placed for the noon photo leaves the seating in full sun at the hour the yard is actually used, which is why the structure usually sits west or southwest of where people sit, set back far enough to block low sun rather than high sun.

Two more things only matter because there is water there. A pool throws reflected light upward, so a structure hard against the coping catches glare and heat under its roof. And a pergola on the wrong axis becomes the permanent view from whichever room faces the yard — worth checking from inside the house before it is staked.
Whether it attaches to the house or stands on its own changes the shade pattern, the drainage and the structure, and that is a decision of its own:
attached versus freestanding
3. The conduit, and the bonding conversation
Everything that makes a pergola worth sitting under is electrical: a fan, lights, a screen motor, speakers, sometimes a TV.

Before the pour, those are sleeves. After it, they are a surface conduit running up a post, or a trench cut across a finished deck. The difference is not subtle and it is decided months before anyone buys a fan.

The part specific to pools is bonding. Aluminum conducts, and metal near pool water belongs to the pool's equipotential bonding grid — a conductor installed under the deck, before it is closed. Adding a metal structure afterwards means either proving the bond already reaches it or creating one, which is an electrician's job and a far easier one while the grid is still exposed. Get the electrician and the pergola installer to agree, in writing, on who ties it in and at what stage. Left implicit, each assumes the other has it.
Pool lighting is priced in our estimator at $450 per fixture. Lighting a pergola is a different system with no line in that table, which is a reason to have it quoted rather than assumed.

blog.alt: Dark bronze aluminum pergola with pale translucent roof panels beside a pool and spa, with a black electrical cable left hanging from the frame where a light fixture will go.

children.text: 4. Where the rain goes

An open slat roof lets rain through and nothing changes. A solid panel or a louvered roof does not, and that is the point of it — but it also takes everything that used to fall across the whole roof and delivers it in a line at one edge.

Three things follow. The roof should not drain toward the pool, or every storm puts roof water and whatever was on the roof into the water you are balancing. Many aluminum systems drain internally through the posts, which is tidy and requires knowing where the post is going before the deck slope is set. And the discharge point has to exist somewhere — a deck poured to drain away from the pool does not automatically have a place for a concentrated flow.
Pool decks are poured with slope in them. That slope is set once.
Four that stay open, and still change the design
5. Roof type: open slats, solid, or louvered
The usual framing is rain protection. Beside a pool there is a better question: do you want the water shaded?

Shaded water is colder water. A pool covered for most of the day in January is a pool that leans on its heater — priced in our estimator at $4,500 — far more often than the neighbor's. Which is why the answer, in most Florida yards, is to shade the people and leave the water in the sun.

That points to a structure set beside the pool rather than over it, and it changes what the roof has to do. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 and a louvered roof at $18,000; the gap is the mechanism and what it buys you is choosing, storm by storm, between sun and cover. Whether that is worth it in your yard is the whole of
pergola versus louvered roof
, and if you are leaning that way,
motorized louvered roof systems
is the build it becomes.
6. The barrier line

A residential pool needs a barrier, and what forms it varies: a fence, a screen enclosure, the house wall with alarmed openings, or some combination. It is drawn on a plan and confirmed at an inspection.

A structure built beside the pool can touch that line. Posts landing next to a fence, a bench or a low wall within reach of it, a roof a barrier ties into — each of those is something a reviewer looks at, not a matter of opinion. The fix is procedural: ask the pergola contractor to show the barrier line on their own drawing, and submit the two together where the county allows it. If the pergola sits inside the barrier, it is a non-issue. If the barrier has to pass around it, that is a thing to design rather than discover.
How the submittal itself works, and what it depends on, is in
do you need a permit for a pergola in Florida

blog.alt: Aluminum patio cover next to a pool, with a removable mesh safety fence, sheets of construction plastic on the grass and a ribbed downspout at the corner of the house.

children.text: 7. What lives underneath, and what the water does to it
The first several feet out from the coping get wet, and not with rainwater. It is treated pool water, arriving as splash and as whatever comes off people walking out.
That zone is where post bases, furniture, rugs, cabinetry and a television end up if the pergola sits close to the pool. Powder-coated aluminum handles it differently from wood, which is most of
how aluminum and wood compare over a Florida decade
. The floor is your deck, priced in our estimator at $12 per square foot in concrete, $22 in pavers and $35 in travertine.
If an
outdoor kitchen
is going under there — $25,000 in the estimator — it brings gas, water and a drain across the same ground as the pool's plumbing, which puts it back in the first section of this list.
8. What the structure has to carry later
A pergola is a frame, and frames get things hung on them for years afterwards.
A ceiling fan needs a beam and a box designed for it, not a bracket added later.
Motorized screens
need track space inside the beam and power at the head. Specified now, it is a detail; retrofitted, it is a different frame.
Heaters, speakers and a projector each want a mounting point and a circuit.
Sizing a structure for something you might add costs very little at the drawing stage. It is the only item on this list that is cheap to over-plan.
What the wrong order actually costs

The pergola line does not move. Our estimator prices it at $8,500 whenever it goes up. The cost of doing it in the wrong order lands entirely on the deck, and how hard it lands was decided by the surface.

Pavers lift, the footing goes in, the pavers reset. There is labor and some breakage, and a seam where the reset batch has weathered differently from the rest. Poured concrete and mortar-set travertine do not lift. They are saw-cut, broken out, footed, and patched — and the patch is visible for as long as the deck exists.

One way to read that: at $12 per square foot for concrete and $22 for pavers, a 600-square-foot deck in pavers costs about $6,000 more. If a pergola, an enclosure or a kitchen is even a possibility later, part of that $6,000 is buying the option to change your mind without cutting the deck open. If the yard is genuinely finished on day one, it is not.
The same logic runs through the rest of the build in
the upgrades worth planning before construction
, which is the pool-side view of this same overlap.
One submittal or two

Our estimator prices permits at 9% of the pool plus the deck. The pergola is not in that base — as a separate structure it generally carries its own review, including the wind and anchoring side, and which department sees it in what order depends on the county rather than on Florida.

What is worth knowing is the shape of it. Two projects a year apart are two submittals, two review cycles and two sets of inspections on overlapping ground. One project is one set of drawings that already shows where the posts, the bonding and the barrier are. Ask who submits, and when.
Turning this into a number
The figures above are the ones behind the site's
pool cost estimator

, and what it returns is a band of roughly ±10% rather than a price, because two identical structures in two different yards are not the same job. What moves the pergola side of that band specifically is in
what changes a pergola's price
; what moves the pool side is in
what a custom pool really costs
Put both into the same number before the meeting. A pergola added to a budget that was fixed around a pool is the classic way an $8,500 line turns into a conversation about cutting the deck.
If you want to see how the two get built as one scope, that is on our
aluminum pergola construction
and
custom pool and spa
pages, there are finished yards in the
project gallery
, and a
project estimate
starts with a site visit rather than a number.

faq.answer: Yes. What changes is the footing. A post carries uplift as well as weight, so it needs a footing sized by the engineer rather than an anchor into a thin deck slab. On a paver deck the pavers lift, the footing goes in and the pavers reset. On poured concrete or mortar-set stone it means saw-cutting and patching.
faq.question: Can I add a pergola to a pool deck that is already finished?

faq.answer: Usually the seating. Shaded water is colder water, and a pool that gets no winter sun leans on its heater far more often. The structure normally goes on the west or southwest side of where people sit, set back far enough that late-afternoon sun is blocked rather than noon sun.
faq.question: Should the pergola shade the pool or the seating area?

faq.answer: A metal structure close to pool water is part of the bonding picture, and the equipotential bonding grid is installed under the deck before it is poured. Ask the electrician and the pergola installer to agree in writing on who ties it in and at what stage, rather than assuming the other one has it.
faq.question: Does an aluminum pergola beside a pool need to be bonded?

faq.answer: It is a separate structure, so it usually carries its own review, including the wind and anchoring side of it. Which department reviews it and in what order depends on the county. The useful question to ask the contractor is who submits it, and whether it goes in with the pool drawings or after them.
faq.question: Does the pergola need its own permit if the pool is already permitted?

summary: A pergola beside a pool is not a pergola that happens to be near water. Four of these eight decisions stop being cheap the day the deck is poured, and the deck material decides how expensive they get.
title: Building a Pergola Beside a Pool? 8 Features Worth Planning Together

children.text: Six of the seven decisions below are locked the day the posts go into concrete. The one about what runs inside the frame is locked earlier than that, when the frame is fabricated. That short window is the whole problem with a pergola: it is a small project next to a pool or a kitchen, it gets decided quickly, and most of the regret afterwards comes from decisions nobody knew they were making.
Take them in the order below. Each one narrows the next, and running them out of order is how a pergola ends up the right size in the wrong place.
When each decision closes

celdas: Saw-cutting, a new footing, a patched slab
Nothing structural, but the shade stays wrong
Re-engineering the frame and the footings
Footings and what they sit in
Surface conduit on a finished frame
Paying for the same footings twice

children.text: Two decisions that are not on this list
Two questions come up first in almost every pergola conversation, and both are large enough to deserve their own answer rather than a paragraph here.
What it is made of.
Aluminum and wood age very differently in Florida humidity, and the comparison is in
aluminum versus wood pergolas over a Florida decade
Whether it touches the house.
Attached and freestanding are different structures with different post counts and different permitting, and that choice is worked through in
attached versus freestanding pergola layouts
Settle both before you start on the seven below. Everything here assumes they are already answered.
1. How big, measured from the furniture rather than the slab
The size of a pergola is not a design preference. It is the output of a furniture plan.

Decide what actually happens under it — a dining table, two loungers, a bar, a grill — and lay it out on the ground with tape before anyone draws a structure around it. Then walk it. Pull a chair back from the table the way people really do and see where your heel lands.
Two things about the numbers on a pergola drawing are worth knowing before you read one:
The outside dimension is not the usable area.

Posts sit inboard of the beam line, and the beams overhang the posts. A structure described as twelve by twenty has a smaller clear span between its posts, and that clear span is what your furniture has to fit inside. Ask for it separately.
The shaded area is smaller than both, and it moves.
A roof throws shade at an angle that changes through the afternoon. At the hours you actually use the space, part of the footprint is in sun. Which hours those are is decision three.

The structure should also be smaller than the paving under it, not the same size. A slab sized exactly to the pergola puts chair legs off the edge, and that is a mistake you notice every time somebody sits down.

blog.alt: Timber pavilion with a gable roof and exposed trusses bolted with steel plates, covering an outdoor kitchen with two built-in grills, a stone island with bar stools and ceiling fans hung along the ridge.

children.text: 2. Where the posts land

A post is the only part of a pergola that is genuinely in your way, and post positions are usually set by the structure rather than by you. That is fine, as long as you check them against how the space is used before the footings are poured.
Five places a post causes a problem, in rough order of how often it happens:
In the walking line between the house door and the pool or the grill.
Inside the swing of a slider or a French door.
At the edge of a pool deck, where it narrows the walkway to a squeeze. If a pool is part of this project,
the features worth planning with a poolside pergola
covers the rest of that overlap.
Centered on a window, so the view from inside the house now has a column in it permanently.
Where the mower and the irrigation have to get past, which is how posts end up with a permanent ring of dead grass around them.
Moving a post on a drawing costs nothing. Moving it after the footing is poured means breaking out concrete, pouring a new footing, and living with a patch in the paving.
The view from inside the house is the one people check last and regret most. Stand at the kitchen sink and the living room sofa, look out, and have somebody hold a broom where each post is going.
3. Which way the shade falls, at the hours you use it
A pergola does not shade a space. It shades part of a space, at particular hours, depending on which way its roof members run.
So the decision starts with a question about your week rather than about the structure:
when will you actually be out there?
Lunch on a Saturday and six o'clock on a Tuesday are different problems, and a roof optimized for one is mediocre at the other.
Three things follow from the answer:
Roof density.

Widely spaced slats read as an open frame and shade very little at midday. Tighter spacing shades more and darkens the space under it. If the hours you named are the hot middle of the day, you are probably looking for more density than the drawing shows.
Which way the slats run.
Fixed slats block sun from one direction better than the other. Running them the wrong way relative to the sun at your hours produces stripes when you wanted shade.
What no roof can fix.
Late afternoon sun comes in low and sideways, under any roof at any density. A west-facing patio at six o'clock is not a roof problem. It is a side problem, solved with planting, a privacy panel, or
motorized retractable screens
— and if screens are even a possibility, that has consequences in decision seven.

The cheapest way to check any of this is to stand on the spot at the hour in question, a week before the drawing is approved. Photographs of finished structures are useful for a different purpose — our
project gallery
shows how the same roof density reads on different houses — but they cannot tell you where your own sun is at five.
4. What the roof does when it rains
There are three families of pergola roof, and the choice between them is not really about how they look. It is about where the water goes.

celdas: Nothing underneath can mind getting wet
Gutter, downspout, and a discharge point
The same, plus a heavier frame and bigger footings

children.text: An open slat roof is a sun structure, not a rain structure. That is a perfectly good thing to build, as long as you know it: a dining table under open slats is fine, and an outdoor kitchen under open slats is an outdoor kitchen in the rain. If appliances are going under this structure, see
what an outdoor kitchen needs from the space around it
before you settle the roof.
The moment the roof sheds water, a second decision appears that most homeowners never get asked about:
where the downspout discharges.

Concentrating a roof's worth of rain next to the house foundation, onto a pool deck, or at the top of a slope toward a neighbor is a worse problem than the one the roof solved. It needs a run of pipe to somewhere that can take it, and that pipe is buried — which means it happens before the paving, not after.

A solid roof also changes the structure itself. It catches wind in a way an open frame does not, which affects the frame, the footings, and what gets reviewed when the drawings are submitted. What that review involves where you live is in
whether a pergola needs a permit in Florida

blog.alt: Attached patio cover with translucent roof panels over a red brick paver patio, with two blue planters and a pair of metal chairs in front of the French doors of a tile-roofed stucco house.

children.text: 5. What it stands on
A patio slab is not a foundation. It is a surface.

Pergola posts have to resist uplift, which is the load that matters for a roof in Florida, and that resistance comes from footings under the posts rather than from the slab around them. On an existing patio, the normal sequence is to saw-cut the slab at each post, dig, pour the footing, and patch. The patch is visible unless the paving can be re-laid over it.
Which gives a simple piece of sequencing that saves real money:
If new paving is part of this project,
the footings go in before the paving is laid, and the patch never exists.
If a pool deck is being poured,
the pergola footings and any sleeves for water, gas or power go in at the same time. The same logic governs the rest of that deck — see
what to plan before a pool deck is poured
If the paving is staying,
budget the cut and the patch openly rather than discovering it as a change order.

How deep and how wide the footings are is an engineering answer for your specific site and structure, not a rule of thumb, and it is one of the things a submitted drawing exists to show. A contractor who can tell you what the footings are and why is a contractor whose drawings have been through that review before.
6. What runs inside the frame
Fans, lights, a heater, speakers, an outlet, a screen motor: every one of them is wire, and on an aluminum pergola the wire runs inside the posts and beams.

That makes it a fabrication decision, not a shopping decision. The frame is cut, drilled and assembled with those runs in it. Adding them afterwards means surface conduit stuck to a finished structure, which is exactly as good as it sounds.
Two details that get missed even when the wiring is planned:
A fan needs structure, not just power.
A fan hangs off a beam and moves while it does it. The beam that carries a fan is specified differently from the beam that holds a light, and that specification happens before anything is cut.
Circuits, not just outlets.
Lights, a couple of fans, a heater and a television are not one circuit. What the panel can give this structure is worth knowing before the trench is dug, because the trench is the expensive part.
The split is the same one that governs pool equipment: you can defer the purchase, you cannot defer the buried half. Buy the fan next year if you want. Put the conduit and the blocking in this year.

blog.alt: Freestanding dark aluminum pergola with translucent roof panels beside a pool, with a slatted privacy panel under it and two thin black cables left hanging from the frame.

children.text: 7. What you are leaving room for
The last decision is about the version of this backyard that exists in three years.
Provisions are cheap while the frame is being made and expensive afterwards. The ones worth asking about:
A column profile and header depth that will accept a
screen track
, whether or not screens are being bought now.
A
gas, water or drain stub
to the corner where a grill or a kitchen would go.
Conduit toward the house
for a controller, a television, or lighting you have not chosen yet.
Enough
footing and frame capacity
for a heavier roof, if the roof might change.

That last one is where the money is. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 and a louvered roof at $18,000 as line items on a backyard project, and the arithmetic looks like it favors starting small. It usually does not, because replacing one structure with the other means paying twice for footings, permitting and installation, and the second set is more expensive than the first — it happens inside a finished yard. If a louvered roof is what you actually want, the comparison to make now rather than later is in
pergola versus louvered roof

Those estimator figures are starting configurations, not quotes, and the estimator shows every total as a range of plus or minus ten percent for exactly that reason. What moves a pergola away from its starting figure — span, roof type, footings, finish — is broken down in
what changes an aluminum pergola's price
. You can run your own combination through the
backyard project estimator
The order, one more time
Settle material and attachment first; they are separate questions.
Lay out the furniture. The footprint comes from it.
Place the posts against doors, walkways, sightlines and the mower.
Name the hours you will use the space, then choose orientation and roof density.
Decide whether the roof sheds water. If it does, decide where the water goes.
Put the footings in before the paving.
Put the wire and the blocking in before the frame is cut, and leave the provisions for later in while it is cheap.

Every one of those seven is permanent once the structure is up. None of them are expensive to get right at the drawing stage, and all of them are expensive to correct afterwards — which is the only real argument for spending an afternoon on a roll of tape and a broom handle before anything is ordered.
How we work through this sequence, and what ends up on the drawing before anything is fabricated, is on the
custom aluminum pergola builders
page. A
project estimate
starts with a site visit, because decisions two through five cannot be made from a floor plan.

faq.answer: The furniture layout. Size and post positions both come out of it, and both are permanent once the footings are poured. Tape the furniture plan onto the slab and stand in it before anyone draws a structure around it.
faq.question: What should I decide first when planning a pergola?

faq.answer: Usually, but the slab is not the foundation. Posts carry uplift and need footings under them, which normally means saw-cutting the slab, digging and pouring, then patching. If you are laying new paving anyway, the footings go in first and the patch never exists.
faq.question: Can a pergola be built on my existing patio slab?

faq.answer: You have to choose whether they are coming. The wiring runs inside the posts and beams, and the beam that carries a fan is not the same beam that holds a light. The fixture itself can be bought later; the conduit and the structure to hang it from cannot be added later without opening the frame.
faq.question: Do I have to choose fans and lights before the pergola is built?

faq.answer: Only if its roof sheds water rather than letting it through. An open slat roof does not. A solid or translucent roof does, and that turns into a second decision most people skip: where the downspout discharges. Next to the house foundation or onto a pool deck is worse than the problem it solved.
faq.question: Does a pergola need gutters?

faq.answer: Only if the upgrade is genuinely years away. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 and a louvered roof at $18,000, but replacing one with the other later also means paying for footings, permitting and installation a second time. If the louvered roof is the real goal, the cheaper path is usually building it once.
faq.question: Should I build a pergola now and upgrade to a louvered roof later?

summary: A pergola is a small project with a very short window. These seven decisions close before anything is built, most of them the day the posts go into concrete, and most people never realize they made them.
title: 7 Pergola Design Decisions to Make Before Construction Starts

children.text: Build the louvered roof if the space underneath has to keep working when it rains. Build the pergola if it does not. Everything else in this comparison — price, permits, drainage, wiring — follows from that one answer, which is why it is worth settling before you look at a single photo.

Both structures are powder-coated aluminum. Both give shade. Both hold up here. The real difference is that a pergola is a fixed filter and a louvered roof is a switch. A pergola's slats sit at the angle they were installed at; a louvered roof's blades rotate, so the same structure is open sky in the morning, full shade at two, and a closed roof when the afternoon storm arrives.
Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 and a motorized louvered roof at $18,000. That gap is the honest starting point. It is also not the whole difference, for reasons further down.
Start with rain, not with shade
Most comparisons open with shade, which is where the two structures are most alike. That is why people read three of them and still cannot decide.

Rain is where they are not alike at all. With the blades closed, a louvered roof is a roof: the panels overlap, the perimeter beams work as gutters, and at least one post carries the water down and out. A pergola does not shed water in any position. Rain goes through it.
So the question is not architectural, it is behavioral:
when a storm arrives at four in the afternoon, does everything under this structure have to keep working?

If what sits underneath is an outdoor kitchen, a television, upholstered furniture, or dinner on the table in August, the answer is yes, and a pergola will disappoint you inside one wet season. If it is a seating area beside the pool that you would be leaving anyway, the answer is no, and the roughly $9,500 difference is buying a capability you will not use. That is the fork, and very little else moves it. What the closed roof does in a real storm — and in wind — is covered in
how a louvered roof behaves in Florida rain and high winds

blog.alt: Louvered roof with white blades tilted partly open in a dark bronze frame, attached to a modern glass-walled house over a concrete patio behind a black pool fence.

children.text: The second question: what time of day do you use it?
Fixed slats block sun coming from overhead. Florida backyards get used late in the day, when the sun is low and coming in from the side, under the structure rather than through it.
Fixed slats do nothing about low sun. Louvers rotate to a steep angle and block it from one direction, which is a different job than shading noon.

This is where a pergola most often disappoints: it is still hot at the hour the space actually gets used. That is not a build-quality problem, it is geometry, and it is solvable while the structure is still on paper — by which way the slats run, by a solid end panel on the west face, or by
planning a screen into the structure from the start
. A screen on one face of a pergola costs far less than a louvered roof and solves the afternoon problem without solving the rain problem. Be clear about which problem you actually have.
What the two prices leave out
The estimator figures above are for the structures. Three things routinely move a louvered roof's real scope, and none of them apply to a pergola:

celdas: Why it only comes up with the louvered roof
The motor needs a dedicated circuit. If the panel is on the far side of the house, that is trenching and conduit, not an extension cord.
Somewhere for the water to go
A closed roof produces runoff, and it leaves at the foot of a post. That discharge point has to be somewhere that genuinely drains.
A closed roof catches wind like a sail. The uplift goes into the footings, so they are bigger and the anchorage is engineered rather than assumed.

children.text: A pergola quote usually lands close to the structure price. A louvered roof quote is the structure price plus a site-dependent amount for those three items. Ask for them as separate lines, or the two numbers you are comparing are not the same kind of number.
Each side has its own breakdown:
what changes a pergola's price
and
what moves the cost of a motorized louvered roof
go through them item by item.
The third structure most comparisons skip

There is something between the two, and for a fair number of backyards it is the right answer: a fixed patio cover — insulated solid panels, or translucent ones — on the same aluminum posts and beams. It sheds rain. It has no motor, no circuit, no actuators, nothing to service. It costs less than a louvered roof.

What it costs you is the sky. Under a solid cover the space is permanently dim. Under translucent panels it is bright, and in July it is hot. Either way you cannot open it on the one February afternoon you want sun on the table.

So if the only reason you were looking at louvers was rain, a fixed cover is a cheaper answer to the same problem. If the reason was control — the same space being different things at different hours — a fixed cover does not do it, and you are back to the louvered roof. That is also the honest version of the
is a motorized louvered roof worth it
question: the motor is worth it when you are buying control, not when you are buying cover.

blog.alt: Attached patio cover with translucent roof panels on a dark aluminum frame over a brick paver patio, a drain grate set into the brick and the barrel-tile roof of the house behind it.

children.text: What fails on each, honestly
A pergola has no moving parts. What ages is the finish, the fasteners and, if it is attached, the connection to the house. Maintenance is washing it.

A louvered roof has motors, actuators, a controller, usually a rain sensor, and seals between the blades. None of it is exotic and all of it is serviceable, but all of it eventually needs service. Two questions are worth asking any installer before you sign:
Who services this system locally, and are they the installer or a third party?
How long do replacement parts take to arrive?

The second answer decides whether a failed actuator is a short inconvenience or a season without a working roof. It predicts how you will feel about the system years from now far better than any spec sheet.

One item specific to here: leaves. Blade seals and the drainage channels in the beams have to be kept clear, and under oaks that is not optional. It is a short job a few times a year — but it is a job somebody has to do.
If you choose the louvered roof, settle these before the posts are set
Where the water discharges.

Not "it drains through the post" — which post, onto what, running where. This is the item most often left for the crew to solve on the day, and it is how a new roof creates a wet corner that was not there before.
Screens, now or never.
Side channels for motorized screens mount to the posts. Deciding later means opening finished work.
The circuit and the controls.
Where the switch lives, whether there is a rain sensor, whether the roof joins whatever already runs the house.
Lights and fans inside the frame.
The beams are hollow. Wiring runs inside them if it was planned and on the surface if it was not, and the difference is visible for as long as the structure stands.
Attached or freestanding
, which changes the footings, the drainage and the permit at once — the trade-offs are in
how the two layouts compare
If you choose the pergola

Two decisions do most of the work: which way the slats run relative to the afternoon sun, and whether the structure attaches to the house. The rest of the sequence — post placement, spans, finish, what the posts land on — is in
the decisions to make before construction starts
. If you are still weighing materials rather than structures,
aluminum against wood over a Florida decade
is the comparison to read first.

One thing to know before you plan around the price: a pergola cannot be converted into a louvered roof later in any economical way. The posts, beams and footings are sized for different loads, and there is no drainage to adapt. If the louvered roof is what you want and the budget is not there this year, building the pergola as a step toward it is the one sequence that does not work.
Deciding in about ten minutes
Answer these out loud:
Does anything under the structure get ruined, or does any plan get cancelled, when it rains? If yes, the pergola is out.
Do you need the space to be different at different hours — sun in February, shade in July? If yes, a fixed cover is out and you are on the louvered roof.
Is the problem specifically the low afternoon sun? That is a screen or an end panel, on either structure.
Is budget the constraint, and was rain the only reason you were considering louvers? Look hard at the fixed panel cover before you compromise on size.

Size is the wrong thing to cut, by the way. A structure that ends up a foot short in each direction stops covering the table it was built for, and that is the one thing you cannot correct once the footings are poured.
Where to take the decision next

With a specific backyard in mind this stops being a spec comparison and becomes a site conversation: how the house sits, where the afternoon sun comes from, what is already under the slab, and where the water can go. Our
aluminum pergola construction
and
motorized louvered roof systems
pages show how each one is built,
the gallery
has both in finished backyards, and a
project estimate
starts with that walk-through rather than with a number.

faq.answer: Not economically. The posts, beams and footings of the two structures are sized for different loads, and a pergola has no drainage to adapt. Building the pergola first as a step toward the louvered roof is the one sequence that does not work.
faq.question: Can a pergola be upgraded to a louvered roof later?

faq.answer: With the blades closed the panels overlap and the water runs to the perimeter beams and down a post, so straight rain stays out. Wind-driven rain still comes in from the open sides, which is what side screens or end panels are for.
faq.question: Does a louvered roof actually keep the space dry?

faq.answer: Both are permitted structures, and the review depends on your county rather than on Florida generally. A closed louvered roof is reviewed as a roof, so its wind uplift, its anchorage and its drainage are all part of the submission. Have the contractor pull the permit under their own license.
faq.question: Do both structures need a permit in Florida?

faq.answer: Little, but not none. The blade seals and the drainage channels in the beams have to be kept clear of leaf litter, which matters under oaks, and the motors and actuators are serviceable parts that eventually need service. Ask who services the system locally before you buy it.

children.text: Build the spa with the pool or do not build it at all, and decide it on the bundle rather than the line item. Our estimator adds
for an integrated spa and
for a spillover spa. But a spa nobody heats is a bench with jets, and the same estimator prices a heater at
. So the real fork is roughly
against nothing — and it closes the day the shell is poured.
Most people arrive at this deciding whether they like the look of a spa. That is a different question, and it is not the one that closes at the pour.
The short version
Build it now if

someone in the house has a concrete reason to want hot water, if the pool is seen from the main living space and the yard has nothing else to look at, or if you are in North Florida, where the spa covers the months the pool does not.
Skip it if

nobody in the house can name a reason to use it beyond "it would be nice", if the yard is tight enough that the spa takes footprint away from the pool, or if the same money does more for how often you actually go outside.
What does not exist
is a cheap middle option. A pool-only build can leave the equipment pad and the electrical sized for a second body of water. It cannot leave the shell ready, and the shell is the expensive half.
Why "we'll add it later" almost never happens
The pool shell is formed and poured as one structure, and if there is a spa it is part of that structure. That single fact is what puts this decision before excavation instead of on a wish list.

Adding a spa to a finished pool means cutting into that shell, tying new steel into cured concrete, running new plumbing back to an equipment pad that was sized for one body of water, and lifting and relaying the deck around all of it. You are not buying a spa at that point. You are buying a demolition, a small construction project and a repair.
There is no line for it in our estimator, and that absence is honest rather than an oversight: it is not a catalog item. For a sense of scale, the estimator prices a complete pool remodel at
of what the same finished result costs as new construction. Having something there already saves less than most people assume.

So ask for two numbers, not one: what the spa costs now, and what it costs to size the equipment pad and the electrical service for a second body of water now. If the second number is small and the first is the problem, that is a real third option. A builder who tells you the shell itself cannot be left ready is being straight with you. Which rough-ins are worth buying up front and which can wait is a decision list of its own — see
the upgrades worth planning before construction
— and the stage each one lands in is in
the pool construction timeline
Integrated or spillover: what the extra $6,000 buys
Both give you the same warm water. The difference is a wall.

celdas: flush with the pool, sharing a wall at deck level
raised above the waterline, water returning over a weir
What you see from the house
a raised wall with a moving sheet of water on it
no water sound of its own
falling water whenever the spillway runs
What it does to the deck
becomes an edge, a seat and a visual stop
nothing blocks the view of the pool
part of the view of the pool is now a wall

children.text: That last row is the one people regret in both directions. Seated on the deck, your eye is close to the top of a raised spa wall, and what is behind it — the far end of the pool — stops being part of the view. Some homeowners find the backyard finally has something to look at; others find they paid to hide water.

So the useful way to spend the $6,000 question is this: if you want a spa because you want warm water, the integrated spa delivers exactly that for $6,000 less. If you want a spa because the view from the kitchen is currently a flat rectangle, you are buying a design element — and then the spillover should be judged against the other things that break up a flat pool, not against no spa at all. A raised bond beam with sheet falls or a planter wall gives the eye the same plane above the water; those are compared side by side in
what makes a pool look custom

blog.alt: Raised spa clad in dark glass tile at the end of a pool, with submerged steps marked by a dark tile band and a travertine deck around them.

children.text: The spa and the heater are one decision

A spa is a small body of water and a pool is a large one. That asymmetry is the entire practical argument for a spa: it is the part of the backyard you can bring to temperature this evening. Moving a whole pool a few degrees is a different proposition in both time and fuel.
Which is why budgeting the spa without the heater produces a number that means nothing. Our estimator prices a heater at

as a single line. What that heater is sized to hold is worth asking about directly — a heater specified around a spa is not automatically one that will keep a whole pool comfortable on a January night in Gainesville or Ocala.
Two operating details that surprise people, and that are much easier to hear now than after the pour:
A spillover spa does not bank its heat.

It shares water with the pool and is isolated by valves only while it heats, so the heater works on the small volume. When the system switches back to pool mode, that heated water goes into the pool. Nothing is wasted, and nothing is stored.
Jets are a pump question, not a spa question.

Ask how many jets there are and what drives them. A spa plumbed off the filtration pump alone does not feel the way a standalone hot tub feels, and the difference between the two is decided on the equipment pad, not in the shell.
Automation
belongs in the same decision. Our estimator prices it at
, and a two-body system is where it earns that: switching to spa mode from a phone half an hour out is the difference between a spa that gets used and one that gets looked at.

blog.alt: Pool with a raised spa in blue mosaic tile on the right and two sheets of water falling from a raised wall on the left, loungers on a travertine deck in the foreground, and tall palms, a golf course and a lake beyond the fence.

children.text: What the same money buys somewhere else

This is the comparison that changes answers, and it is the one that rarely gets run. The spa is not competing with "no spa". It is competing with everything else the yard could have, out of the same budget. All of these are estimator figures:

celdas: Instead of a spillover spa at $18,000
The full equipment package: heater, salt chlorination, automation and four LED lights

children.text: Look at the third row. Heater, salt system, automation and four lights come to
— the whole equipment specification for a pool you will swim in year round, for a third less than the spillover spa alone.

None of this makes the spa the wrong answer. It makes the spa one of four or five things, rather than an upgrade you either take or leave. And it is the only one on that list whose window closes at the pour — although the
screen enclosure
has its own timing rule, because the deck has to be built to carry it whether or not it goes up on day one. That, and the eleven other decisions in the same bracket, are in
the twelve decisions to make before excavation

blog.alt: Overhead view of a rectangular pool with a square spa set into it, water spilling over the spa rim on all four sides in a band of white foam, on a travertine deck with handrails at the pool edges and a lounger and blue umbrella at the bottom of the frame.

children.text: The question that actually settles it
Not "do we want a spa". This one:
how many evenings a year will someone in this house sit in hot water?
Ask it out loud, with the people who live there. The honest answer is usually smaller than the one in your head, and it is the number the rest of the decision runs on.
Geography moves that number more than anything else. North Florida gets a real winter, and in
Gainesville
and
Ocala

the weeks when the pool is too cold to enjoy are the weeks a spa gets used. That is a spa doing a job. Further south the job is different: jets, a smaller space for two people, a focal point from the house in the evening. All real, all worth paying for if that is what you want — but they are not the same argument, and a spa bought on the North Florida argument in a South Florida yard tends to become a heated planter.
If the honest count comes back at a handful of nights, the money usually belongs in whatever makes you use the pool more often: shade, screening, or somewhere to cook and sit.
Three cases where it is already decided
Someone has a physical reason to want hot water
— a back, a joint, a training schedule. Build it. Skip the whether conversation entirely and spend it on jet count and pump instead.
The pool is the whole backyard, and you see it from where you live.
The spillover spa is doing double duty as the view, and the $18,000 is buying a design element as much as a soak. That is a defensible purchase.
The yard is tight.

A spa and a pool compete for the same footprint. A pool that loses width so the spa fits is a worse pool every day of the year in exchange for something used a few evenings of it. Pool only, and put the money into finish or deck — both of which you touch every time you go outside.
What the spa does not change
Permitting.
The spa is designed, reviewed and inspected as part of the pool rather than as its own project, which is why our estimator calculates permit cost as
of the pool and deck rather than adding a separate line for the spa. Whoever builds it should permit it under their own license and be present for the inspections.
The schedule, materially.

A spa does not add a stage. It makes the existing ones slightly bigger, because it is excavated, formed, poured, tiled and finished along with the pool. The part that does affect your schedule is the equipment and automation, which arrive late and are a common place a project waits.
The rest of the design.
Finish, deck material and deck size are priced independently, and all three are covered decision by decision in
what a custom pool really costs
What to do with this

Settle three things before your design is final: spa or no spa, integrated or spillover if yes, and how it is heated and jetted. That is the whole decision, and it wants to be made once, on paper, before anyone ties steel.
Then run it twice through
our pool cost estimator
— once with the spa, once without — and look at what the spa does to the total rather than at the line by itself. What comes out is a
range, not a quote, and it is meant to tell you which decision is moving your number.
Bring both versions to the site visit. A
project estimate

starts by reviewing access, grade and utilities rather than by quoting a number, and seeing the two scopes side by side is the fastest way to find out which one you actually want. How the process runs from there is on the
custom pool and spa construction
page, and there are finished pools and spas in
the gallery

faq.answer: Physically yes, but it is not an upgrade, it is demolition plus new construction. The spa shares structure with the pool, so adding one means cutting into a finished shell, tying new steel into old, and running new plumbing back to an equipment pad that was sized for one body of water. There is no line for it in our estimator because it is priced per site, not from a catalog.
faq.question: Can I add a spa to my pool later?

faq.answer: An integrated spa sits flush with the pool and shares a wall with it. A spillover spa is raised above the waterline and returns water over a weir. Our estimator adds $12,000 for the first and $18,000 for the second. The water is the same temperature either way; the extra buys a raised structure, the falling water and the sound.
faq.question: What is the difference between an integrated spa and a spillover spa?

faq.answer: If the reason you want a spa is warm water, then yes, and the two should be budgeted as one decision rather than two. Our estimator prices a heater at $4,500. What that heater is sized to hold is worth asking about directly, because a heater chosen around a spa is not automatically one that will keep a whole pool comfortable in January.
faq.question: Do I need a heater if I build a spa?

faq.answer: No. A spillover spa shares water with the pool and is isolated by valves only while it heats. When the system returns to pool mode that heated water goes into the pool, so the spa is not warm tomorrow because it was warm tonight. Nothing is wasted, but nothing is stored either.
faq.question: Does a spillover spa keep its heat between uses?

faq.answer: It depends on why you would use it. North Florida has a real winter, and there the spa covers the months the pool does not. Further south the case is usually jets, a smaller space for two people, and something to look at from inside the house. Those are legitimate reasons — they are just different ones, and they are worth naming before you spend on them.

strict regulations
, humid climate, and sandy soils demand a precise timeline to avoid costly setbacks.

planning and permits
(Weeks 1-8) through excavation, installation, finishing, and final testing-spanning
4-6 months

children.text: Florida pool construction

typically spans 4-6 months from consultation to first swim, with permitting delays averaging 4-6 weeks per Florida DBPR data. This timeline covers seven key phases for a standard inground pool project. Each phase includes specific week ranges and milestones to help homeowners plan ahead.
Phase 1 (
weeks 1-2
): Design consultation and soil testing ensure site suitability. Phase 2 (weeks 3-8): Permitting and approvals handle Florida-specific regulations. Phase 3 (
weeks 9-10
): Excavation and site preparation shape the pool footprint.
Phase 4 (
weeks 11-13
): Rebar installation and gunite application form the shell. Phase 5 (
weeks 14-18
): Plumbing rough-in, electrical rough-in, and equipment setup follow. Phase 6 (weeks 19-22): Tile installation, coping, and deck pouring complete finishes.
Phase 7 (
weeks 23-24
): Startup process, inspections, and punch list finalize the build. A Gantt chart example below shows the
critical path
, highlighting overlaps in rough-ins and finishes. Reference the 2023 Florida Building Code Chapter 45 for pool standards.

Imagine a sample Gantt chart with bars for each phase: permitting as the longest early bar, excavation short and sequential, gunite critical with no float time, decking overlapping startup. For a 15x30ft gunite pool, expect an
average cost timeline of $80K-$150K
, spread across materials, labor, and delays.
Florida-Specific Regulations and Permits
Florida requires
CPC-licensed contractors
(DBPR verified) and compliance with 2023 Florida Building Code Chapter 45 for pools, including 4ft barrier fencing. These rules ensure safety and durability, especially for
hurricane-resistant pools
. Homeowners must verify licenses early to avoid delays.
Key requirements include six main items. First, check CPC license via myfloridalicense.com. Second, install pool barriers with
48in minimum height
and self-closing gates.
Third, obtain a
structural engineering stamp

for plans. Fourth, follow electrical GFCI per NEC 680 for all outlets. Fifth, secure HOA or zoning approval, often taking 30-45 days. Sixth, pass health department plan review for public safety features.

Professional design phase establishes
pool dimensions
, features, and engineering compliance using AutoCAD and Pool Studio software (4-week minimum).
Contractors start with
site surveys
and concept sketches in Week 1 to map out the space. Week 2 brings detailed
3D renderings
using Vip3D for visualizing features like an

or

. These tools help clients see the final look before any digging begins.
In Week 3, teams prepare

with a structural stamp to meet Florida codes. Week 4 finalizes

and the contract, locking in details such as a
beach entry
slope. This phase sets the foundation for smooth inground pool installation.

Site Assessment and Soil Testing
Geotechnical soil testing identifies Florida's
sandy or clay composition
, addressing common issues like settlement. Experts use standard methods to evaluate the site. This step prevents problems during later pool construction steps.
The process follows five key assessment steps.
Topographic survey
(1-2 days) maps elevation changes and slopes.
Soil borings
(4-6ft depth) sample underground layers.
Percolation test
checks water drainage rates.
Tree root analysis
identifies potential obstructions from palms or oaks.
Engineering report
summarizes findings with recommendations.
Florida sites often face
high water tables
or coral rock, requiring special footings. Reference the FDOT soil manual for local guidelines on handling these conditions.

Match soil type to

, such as deeper pilings in rocky areas, ensuring compliance with Florida swimming pool regulations.
Phase 2: Permitting and Approvals (Weeks 4-8)
Permitting averages 4-6 weeks in Florida counties. Delays often occur during the
rainy season
from June to October. Pool builders submit documents early to stay on track with the overall
pool construction timeline
The process starts with submitting
engineered plans
to the county. County review takes about two to three weeks. After that, revisions may need one week before final
pool permit approval
Key agencies involved include the
County Building Department
, Health Department, Zoning Board, and HOA. Each reviews for compliance with Florida pool codes and local rules. Coordinating with all helps avoid setbacks in
Florida pool building
County Building Department: Checks structural safety and building standards.
Health Department: Ensures water quality and sanitation features.
Zoning Board: Verifies setbacks and land use rules.
HOA: Confirms community guidelines for design and barriers.
A common documents checklist covers
site plan
, truss engineering, and barrier detail. These prove the pool meets pool safety features like fencing. Missing items can extend the
swimming pool project phases
In a Miami-Dade case study, a
gunite pool
gained approval in six weeks. The builder prepared detailed pool engineering plans upfront. This kept the
inground pool installation
moving smoothly despite reviews.

Excavation removes 150-200 cubic yards for a standard
15x30ft pool
using a
30-ton excavator
over 2-3 days of labor. This phase marks the

in your pool construction timeline. Contractors follow a precise 5-step process to ensure accuracy.
First, they mark the
pool outline
with batter boards and string lines. Next comes

, digging about 6 inches deeper than needed. This allows room for adjustments during later steps.
Utility exposes follow to check for hidden lines. Then, a
precision dig
uses laser levels for exact depth and shape. Finally,

reaches 95% Proctor density to create a stable base.
Safety requires shoring trenches deeper than
5ft

utilities. Contractors follow a strict procedure to comply with Florida Statute 556.

Phase 4: Steel and Plumbing Installation (Weeks 10-12)

children.text: Grade 60 rebar (#4 at 8in OC)
forms pool shell per ACI 318, with plumbing rough-in using
Schedule 40 PVC
. This phase strengthens the structure and sets up water circulation. Contractors schedule it after excavation and formwork settle.
Steel installation spans
days 1-3

of the phase. Teams lay the bottom grid first, then erect wall grids, securing everything with tie wire. This rebar installation ensures the pool withstands Florida's soil shifts and hurricane forces.
Plumbing rough-in follows on
days 4-5
. Workers install the main drain, skimmers, returns, and sweep manifold. These components form the backbone of the
pool plumbing rough-in
, vital for efficient filtration.
Florida pool codes require a
bonding grid
using 8AWG copper wire. Inspectors check photo milestones at key steps, like grid completion and pipe tests. This verifies compliance before gunite application.
Rebar Specifications for Steel Reinforcement
Rebar spacing follows strict guidelines for pool construction steps. The shell uses
#4 rebar at 8 inches on center
, while the deck needs

. These sizes provide tensile strength against ground pressure.

integrity. Experts recommend verifying grade 60 certification on site. This prevents cracks in the inground pool installation.
During rainy season, crews protect grids from corrosion. A structural engineer often stamps plans for
Florida building permits

The
main drain

Main drain with

Returns direct water circulation to avoid dead spots.
Sweep manifold supports

All pipes use Schedule 40 PVC glued with proper primer. Unions allow future service, and valves control flow in the manifold. Pressure tests confirm no leaks before covering.
In Florida pool building, bonding ties plumbing to the grid for safety. This meets NEC codes and
pool safety features
requirements. Inspectors review photos to approve progression.
Phase 5: Gunite/Shotcrete and Forming (Weeks 12-14)
4000psi gunite

at 4in min walls, 6in floor applied at 1500psi via 1.5in nozzle marks a 2-day pour in this critical pool construction timeline. Crews use plywood forms to shape the inground pool installation. This phase builds the durable shell for your Florida swimming pool project.
Wall forms go up first, securing
steel reinforcement
from prior steps.
Gunite crews
spray the mix with precision for even coverage. The process demands skilled labor to meet Florida pool codes.
Curing follows for seven days under wet conditions to gain strength. Forms strip away after, revealing the solid structure. Expect

checks here for quality.

. Florida wind load forming adds extra bracing for hurricane-resistant pools. These steps ensure the concrete pool schedule stays on track.

Plywood
wall forms
erect around the excavated shape, braced against Florida's wind loads. They hold the position for gunite application. Proper alignment prevents shifts during the pour.
Crews check rebar installation for coverage before sealing forms. Ties and supports secure everything. This prep sets up a smooth
shotcrete pool shell
Experts recommend verifying form tightness to avoid leaks. Use
form release agent

Gunite Crews and Application
Gunite crews arrive for the intense 2-day pour, nozzle in hand. They build walls and floor in layers for strength. Timing keeps the mix fresh during swimming pool project phases.
The high-pressure spray compacts material against forms and steel. Nozzles stay clean for consistent flow. Watch for even thickness to match design specs.
Coordination with pool contractor timeline avoids delays. Crews work in teams for efficiency. This phase transforms the dig into a pool shape.
Curing and Form Stripping
After pouring,
curing time
starts with seven days of wet coverage. Burlap or plastic sheets keep moisture in for proper hardening. Avoid foot traffic during this period.
Forms strip once cured, exposing the raw shell. Inspect for cracks or voids right away. Backfill
pool walls
follows if needed.
Proper curing boosts durability against Florida's climate. Schedule pool inspection schedule post-strip. This readies for plumbing and finishes in the

Electrical rough-in with

, tile and coping work begins here, followed by the 4-inch paver or concrete deck pour done concurrently. This phase wraps up the pool construction timeline in Florida, focusing on safety and aesthetics. Crews wire lights, pumps, and heaters while installing finishes.
In week 14, electricians handle rough-in and

. Tiles go on walls and floors for a watertight, decorative surface. Compliance with

Weeks

Florida mandates

Inspections follow a clear sequence in the pool inspection schedule. First, pre-gunite verifies rebar and plumb lines. Post-gunite inspects the shell for cracks or issues.

The
startup checklist

equipment wiring

After wiring, a full

The phase ends with a detailed

. Homeowners learn basic operations during this time. Expect minor adjustments in the first weeks post-fill.
Startup Checklist
Equipment wiring
: Confirm all connections for pumps, heaters, lights, and automation systems meet NEC and Florida pool codes, including GFCI protection.
Filter charge
: Load DE powder or sand into the filter, prime the system, and check for proper backwash function.
System test run
: Run pumps at various speeds, test valves, sweeps, and heaters to ensure no unusual noises or leaks.
Fill and chemical balance

Walkthrough

This ordered process minimizes issues during the

children.text: The decisions that make an old pool feel new are the ones that change what you
do

in the yard, not the ones that change what you look at. Ranked that way, the list opens with how many months the water is warm enough to get into, what shades the deck between noon and five, and whether there is anywhere to sit other than a lounger. The interior finish, which is where nearly every remodel conversation starts, comes ninth.
That is one ranking of the same work, and it is worth saying which one it is.
Which changes you actually see from the deck
ranks this list by what reads in the view.
What belongs in the scope while the pool is open

sorts it by what closes when the crew leaves. This article asks a third question, and it is the one people are actually paying to answer: after everybody has gone home, what is different about a Saturday?

The remodel worth avoiding is the one that changes everything you look at and nothing you do. New tile, new coping, new plaster — and the water is still too cold in March, the deck is still unusable at two in the afternoon, and the same two people get in.
The nine, in order

celdas: Heat, and how much water you heat
Months of the year the pool gets used
Hours of the day the deck gets used
Who uses the pool, not just how often
Whenever there are more than two of you
What upkeep costs and feels like
Whether you sit outside at night, and how it gets serviced
Nightly, and at every service call
How the pool reads, and what you grab and sit on
Every time you look at it or get out
Whether the pool has an evening at all
Texture underfoot, and when you do this again
Daily, and again at the next refinish

children.text: The three that decide how often anyone gets in
1. Heat, and how much water you are heating
A heater is a purchase. Our estimator prices one at
, and it can be bought in any year without a remodel. What cannot be bought later is a pool that is cheap to heat, and three remodel decisions set that permanently.
Volume.

A diving well nobody has used since the children left is water kept at the same temperature as the water people are standing in. Filling it is a structural decision taken before demolition, and it changes the heating load and the chemical demand for the rest of the pool's life.
Exposure.

Sun on the water is free heat. This is also the decision that fights with the next one on the list: the tree or structure that makes the deck usable in August is the reason the water is cold in February. Decide both at once or you will win one and lose the other.
Whether the spa can run on its own.

A spa that can be isolated and heated by itself is usable on a cold evening. A spa that shares the pool's body of water costs the whole pool's heat to use, which in practice means it does not get used. That is a plumbing and valve decision made during the remodel, not an equipment decision made afterwards.

blog.alt: Raised spa clad in small white tile with its jets running, beside a rectangular pool with two white loungers standing on the deck at the top of its wide entry steps, and two grills under the covered lanai behind.

children.text: 2. What shades the deck between noon and five
A deck too hot to cross barefoot is not a deck, and a pool nobody walks to is not used. Deck material is priced per square foot in our
pool cost estimator
and surface temperature varies with it, but the larger lever is what stands over the deck rather than what it is made of.
Three scopes, all priced in the estimator: a
pergola at $8,500
, a
screen enclosure at $15,000
, a
motorized louvered roof at $18,000
. They do different jobs. A
pergola
shades at a fixed angle, so where it sits decides which hours it is worth having. A
louvered roof
lets you change that angle and close it in rain. A
screen enclosure
changes insects and leaf load far more than it changes heat, which is a different problem that often gets solved with the wrong product.

The part worth doing before anyone draws anything: stand in the yard at four in the afternoon, in the month you use the pool most, and mark where the shadow of the house actually falls. Shade gets designed on plan at noon, because noon is the easiest geometry and the sun is overhead — and noon is not when anybody is out there. Anything standing over the deck also needs footings through the slab, which is why
the timing belongs with the rest of the scope

blog.alt: Rectangular pool with a shallow shelf at the near end and a travertine paver deck, a basketball hoop at the far edge, a covered lanai with ceiling fans to the left and palms behind a black metal fence.

children.text: 3. Where people can sit, in the water and on the deck
Most old pools offer exactly two positions: swimming, or sitting on a lounger looking at the water. The edits that change that are cuts into the shell, so they are decided before demolition:
A shallow ledge
, which is where people who do not swim spend the afternoon, and where a small child stays within arm's reach.
A bench along a wall
, which is what keeps adults in the water for an hour instead of ten minutes.
A wider, shallower entry step
in place of a ladder. This is the decision that determines whether a grandparent gets in at all, and it is almost never on anybody's list.
A raised wall
, which is also the thing a spout or spillway has to be built into later.

The deck half of the same question is width, not material. A uniform walkway around a pool has nowhere to put a table, because a table needs the depth of a chair pulled out plus a path to walk behind it. Measure the furniture you already own before anyone quotes a surface: pull a chair out from your indoor table, measure what it occupies, and mark that on the ground. Widening one side and narrowing another can cost the same square footage. What that does to the view is covered in
the changes you actually see
; what it does to the slab and its drainage is
custom deck construction

blog.alt: Pool with two white chaise loungers standing in its shallow shelf, a spa trimmed in dark blue tile at the near left, a pale stone deck around both, and a single-story house with a covered lanai behind.

children.text: The three you never look at and notice every week
Nothing in this group shows up in a photograph. Together they are most of what people mean when they say a pool is easy, or that it is a pain.
4. How the water actually moves

You can diagnose an old pool's circulation without touching the equipment. The same corner is always the last to clear after a storm. One end is noticeably warmer than the other on a heated day. The water behind the steps never seems to move at all.

That is geometry, not chemistry — how many returns there are and where they point — and it gets blamed on the sanitizer for years. It costs a homeowner in brushing time, in chemical, and in the one corner that always goes green first. Ask where the returns are and where they aim
before
the finish is specified, because both are cut into the shell.

Pipe diameter belongs in the same conversation. How quietly and how cheaply a variable-speed pump can turn the pool over depends on the diameter it is pushing water through, and that diameter was decided the day the pool was plumbed. The pump is a purchase you can make in any year. What it pushes against is not.
5. Where the equipment lives, and how loud it is
The pad went where the plumbing run was shortest on the day the pool was built. Two decades later it is under a bedroom window, or on the side of the house you now want to use for something else.

Noise is the consequence people notice: a pad you can hear from the deck is a pad you turn off in the evening, which is the half of the day you were hoping to get back. Service access is the consequence they notice later. A pad you cannot reach with a filter cartridge in both hands is a pad that gets serviced badly, and that shows up as equipment life rather than as an inconvenience.

Decide it against three things: what it is audible from, what will screen it, and whether there is room to stand in front of it. The screening is the part that gets forgotten, because it belongs to a different trade —
landscaping
has to know where the pad ended up before anything gets planted in front of it.
6. Sanitizing, and who decides when the pool runs
Our estimator prices salt chlorination at
and automation at
. Neither changes a single thing about how the pool looks, and between them they change the weekly routine more than anything else on this list.
On a scope list they belong near the bottom, because neither needs the shell, the deck or the trench open — that is the argument in
what belongs in the scope while the pool is open
, and it is correct. On this list they are sixth, because the bottom of a scope list is not the bottom of a difference. They are cheap to defer and worth having.

One thing in this group is trapped by the remodel: the electrical capacity and the conduit at the pad. Confirm that both can carry whatever you might add while there is an electrician on site, or the inexpensive upgrade turns into a trench.
The three that decide what you look at, and when you do this again
7. The edge: coping and waterline tile
This is the one item where the visual ranking and this one agree, and
the changes you actually see

covers what the tile band and the coping profile do to the view. The part that belongs here is narrower and gets left out of both conversations: the coping is the edge you grab when you get out, sit on with your feet in the water, and walk on wet.

Profile is therefore a comfort decision as much as a visual one. A square or cantilevered edge is a better handhold and a harder thing to sit on for twenty minutes. A rolled bullnose is the opposite. Whichever you choose, choose it with a hand and a wet foot rather than from a sample board, because you will use it that way every time.
8. Light
Our estimator prices LED pool lights at
$450 each

. That number is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that in Florida the comfortable hours in summer are after dark, so a pool without usable light is a daytime object in the season when daytime is the worst time to be outside. Lighting is an hours-of-use decision, and it belongs in the same argument as heating rather than in the argument about photographs.

An older pool typically has one large fixture in the deep end aimed back at the house. It lights the water from one side, leaves the shallow end dark, and shines directly at whoever is sitting on the far deck. More fixtures and better aim fix all three. A pool fixture is not a lamp you screw in: the wall is formed around its housing and a conduit run back to power, which makes the count and the aiming a shell decision rather than an equipment one.
The exception worth knowing is lighting mounted on the house itself, like
permanent soffit LED lighting
, which is not trapped by the deck at all. That is a reason to decide it separately and later, not a reason to leave the yard dark.
9. The interior finish, and what you are buying with it
Our estimator multiplies the pool line by
1 for plaster, 1.15 for pebble and 1.35 for a premium finish
. The color conversation dominates this decision and two things it leaves out matter more day to day.
Texture.

An exposed-aggregate finish has more grip than plaster and more bite — better on a step you walk down wet, more abrasive under a foot resting on a ledge for an hour. If decision 3 gave you a ledge people will stand on daily, feel the sample with a bare foot, not with a hand.
Service life.

The finish is the item that decides when the pool next comes offline, which is to say when you do some version of this again. It also cannot be deferred at all: once the pool is drained it is being refinished, whatever else is or is not in the scope.
Color still matters, and how it reads against the coping and the deck is in
the changes you actually see
. Ask to see any candidate in finished water, outdoors, at a depth close to yours. Samples are dry, small and lit by a showroom.
The pairs that have to be decided together
Most of the regret in a remodel is not a bad decision. It is two good decisions taken separately.

celdas: To fill the unused diving well
What the pool costs to heat from then on
To shade the west side of the deck
That the water gets less of the afternoon sun that heats it
Where a bubbler could ever go, and where sun has to reach for the ledge to be worth having
What has to screen it, and which side of the house stays quiet
To widen one side of the deck
The permit line, which our estimator calculates at 9% of the pool and deck work

children.text: That last row surprises people. Permitting scales with scope rather than arriving as a flat fee, and what gets reviewed is a county question rather than a Florida one — a cosmetic resurface, a structural change to the shell and new electrical are three different submissions.
What permits are required for pool work in Florida

walks through a full set. Whatever your scope turns out to be, the work should be permitted and inspected under a licensed contractor, and you can check that license yourself in the state's public registry.
What to do with this before anyone quotes it
Walk the yard twice on the same day

— once between three and five, once after dark. Mark where the shade is and where the light is not. Those two walks settle decisions 2 and 8, which are the two most often decided from a plan drawing by people who have never stood in the yard at those hours.
Write one sentence per decision
saying what changes about a Saturday. Any decision you cannot finish that sentence for belongs lower than you currently have it, and the money belongs somewhere else.
Then price it.
Every figure quoted above is one the
pool cost estimator

works from, and what it hands back is a band at plus or minus 10% rather than a single number. That is deliberate: in a remodel the real variable is the condition of what is already there, and nobody knows that — us included — until the shell is exposed.
Two things sit outside this list.
What actually changes a remodel's scope
is where the arithmetic lives, and whether the existing shell is worth keeping at all is a decision taken before any of these nine, in
remodel or rebuild
. If you want to see how the nine land in finished work rather than in renderings,
our project gallery
is built jobs.
The way we scope a
complete pool remodel
follows the order above, starting from what the existing shell, deck and plumbing can carry. To turn a scope into a price,
request an estimate
— and ask for the visit at the hour you would actually be out there.

faq.answer: A change in what you do in the yard, not only in what you look at. The pool gets used more months of the year, the deck is usable in the afternoon, and there is somewhere to sit other than a lounger. A pool can be entirely refinished and still be used exactly as little as before.
faq.question: What actually makes an old pool feel new?

faq.answer: It makes it look clean, which is not the same thing. Resurfacing changes nothing about when the pool is warm enough to use, whether the deck is usable at two in the afternoon, or where a person can sit in the water. Those are separate decisions with separate scopes.
faq.question: Does resurfacing alone make an old pool look new?

faq.answer: Partly. A concrete shell can be cut and added to, so edits at the edges are practical — a tanning ledge, a bench, a wider entry step, a raised wall, filling an unused diving well. Changing the overall outline is a different project, and at that point the honest comparison is against building new.
faq.question: Can you change the shape of an existing pool?

faq.answer: Our estimator prices a full remodel at about 82% of what the same finished result costs as new construction, because the excavation and the shell already exist. That assumes the existing shell is sound; if it is not, the comparison changes.
faq.question: Is a pool remodel cheaper than building new?

faq.answer: It depends on the scope and on the county, which is why the answer varies across Florida. A cosmetic resurface, a structural change to the shell and new electrical or plumbing are different reviews. Whatever the scope, the work should be permitted and inspected under a licensed contractor, and you can confirm that license in the state's public registry.
